# rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/

## Expand description

Generating random samples from probability distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-exports)Re-exports

This crate is a super-set of the [ rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html) module. See the

[module documentation for an overview of the core](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html)

`rand::distr`[trait and implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)

`Distribution`The following are re-exported:

- The `Distribution``Iter`
- The `StandardUniform``Alphanumeric``Uniform``OpenClosed01``Open01``Bernoulli`
- The `weighted`

[§](https://docs.rs#distributions)Distributions

This crate provides the following probability distributions:

- Related to real-valued quantities that grow linearly
(e.g. errors, offsets):
- `Normal`- `StandardNormal`
- `SkewNormal`
- `Cauchy`

- Related to Bernoulli trials (yes/no events, with a given probability):
- `Binomial`
- `Geometric`
- `Hypergeometric`

- Related to positive real-valued quantities that grow exponentially
(e.g. prices, incomes, populations):
- `LogNormal`

- Related to the occurrence of independent events at a given rate:
- Gamma and derived distributions:
- `Gamma`
- `ChiSquared`
- `StudentT`
- `FisherF`

- Triangular distribution:
- `Beta`
- `Triangular`

- Multivariate probability distributions
- `multi::Dirichlet`
- `UnitSphere`
- `UnitBall`
- `UnitCircle`
- `UnitDisc`

- Misc. distributions
- `InverseGaussian`
- `NormalInverseGaussian`

- Weighted (index) sampling

- The standard geometric distribution `Geometric(0.5)`.

- The Standard Uniform distribution

- [Triangular](https://docs.rs/struct.Triangular.html)
- The [triangular distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_distribution)`Triangular(min, max, mode)`.
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)
- Sample values uniformly between two bounds.
- [Unit](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitBall.html)- Ball
- Samples uniformly from the volume of the unit ball in three dimensions.
- [Unit](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitCircle.html)- Circle
- Samples uniformly from the circumference of the unit circle in two dimensions.
- [Unit](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitDisc.html)- Disc
- Samples uniformly from the unit disc in two dimensions.
- [Unit](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitSphere.html)- Sphere
- Samples uniformly from the surface of the unit sphere in three dimensions.
- [Weibull](https://docs.rs/struct.Weibull.html)
- The [Weibull distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution)`Weibull(λ, k)`.
- [Zeta](https://docs.rs/struct.Zeta.html)
- The [Zeta distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_distribution)`Zeta(s)`.
- [Zipf](https://docs.rs/struct.Zipf.html)
- The Zipf (Zipfian) distribution `Zipf(n, s)`.

# rand_distr 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/latest

# rand_distr

Implements a full suite of random number distribution sampling routines.

This crate is a superset of the [rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/distr/index.html) module, including support
for sampling from Beta, Binomial, Cauchy, ChiSquared, Dirichlet, Exponential,
FisherF, Gamma, Geometric, Hypergeometric, InverseGaussian, LogNormal, Normal,
Pareto, PERT, Poisson, StudentT, Triangular and Weibull distributions.  Sampling
from the unit ball, unit circle, unit disc and unit sphere surfaces is also
supported.

It is worth mentioning the [statrs](https://github.com/statrs-dev/statrs) crate which provides similar functionality
along with various support functions, including PDF and CDF computation. In
contrast, this `rand_distr` crate focuses on sampling from distributions.

## Portability and libm

The floating point functions from `num_traits` and `libm` are used to support
`no_std` environments and ensure reproducibility. If the floating point
functions from `std` are preferred, which may provide better accuracy and
performance but may produce different random values, the `std_math` feature
can be enabled. (Note that any other crate depending on `num-traits` with the
`std` feature (default-enabled) will have the same effect.)

## Crate features

- `std`(enabled by default):- `rand_distr`implements the- `Error`trait for its error types. Implies- `alloc`and- `rand/std`.
- `alloc`(enabled by default): required for some distributions when not using- `std`(in particular,- `Dirichlet`and- `WeightedAliasIndex`).
- `std_math`: see above on portability and libm
- `serde`: implement (de)seriaialization using- `serde`

## Links

## Old Issues and Pull Requests

- All closed Issues and merged Pull requests from before 5.February.2025 (version 0.5.0) can be found in the [rand](https://github.com/rust-random/rand)repository where this crate used to be.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.10.0/

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.166/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# serde_with - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_with/^3/

## Expand description

This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with) and with the improved

[-annotation. Some common use cases are:](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/serde_as/index.html)

`serde_as`- De/Serializing a type using the `Display`and`FromStr`traits, e.g., for`u8`,`url::Url`, or`mime::Mime`. Check`DisplayFromStr`
- Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
With `serde_as`large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.`[bool; 64]`,`Option<[u8; M]>`, and`Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>`are all supported, as[this examples shows](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
- Skip serializing all empty `Option`types with`#[skip_serializing_none]`
- Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using `with_prefix!``with_suffix!`
- Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great`into a`Vec<String>`. Check the documentation for`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-help)Getting Help

**Check out the  user guide to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**

For further help using this crate you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-serde_with-in-your-project)Use `serde_with` in your Project

```
# Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
cargo add serde_with
```
The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
Check the [feature flags](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/feature_flags/index.html) section for information about all available features.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#displayfromstr)`DisplayFromStr`

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    // Serialize with Display, deserialize with FromStr
    #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
    bar: u8,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {bar: 12}
// into this JSON
{"bar": "12"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays)Large and const-generic arrays

serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.

On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Arrays<const N: usize, const M: usize> {
    #[serde_as(as = "[_; N]")]
    constgeneric: [bool; N],
    #[serde_as(as = "Box<[[_; 64]; N]>")]
    nested: Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Option<[_; M]>")]
    optional: Option<[u8; M]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Bytes")]
    bytes: [u8; M],
}
// This allows us to serialize a struct like this
let arrays: Arrays<100, 128> = Arrays {
    constgeneric: [true; 100],
    nested: Box::new([[111; 64]; 100]),
    optional: Some([222; 128]),
    bytes: [0x42; 128],
};
assert!(serde_json::to_string(&arrays).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#skip_serializing_none)`skip_serializing_none`

This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

```
#[skip_serializing_none]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    a: Option<usize>,
    b: Option<usize>,
    c: Option<usize>,
    d: Option<usize>,
    e: Option<usize>,
    f: Option<usize>,
    g: Option<usize>,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {a: None, b: None, c: None, d: Some(4), e: None, f: None, g: Some(7)}
// into this JSON
{"d": 4, "g": 7}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-serde_as-usage)Advanced `serde_as` usage

This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with).
More details about

`serde_as` can be found in the [user guide](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/index.html).

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
enum Foo {
    Durations(
        // Serialize them into a list of number as seconds
        #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DurationSeconds>")]
        Vec<Duration>,
    ),
    Bytes {
        // We can treat a Vec like a map with duplicates.
        // JSON only allows string keys, so convert i32 to strings
        // The bytes will be hex encoded
        #[serde_as(as = "Map<DisplayFromStr, Hex>")]
        bytes: Vec<(i32, Vec<u8>)>,
    }
}
// This will serialize
Foo::Durations(
    vec![Duration::new(5, 0), Duration::new(3600, 0), Duration::new(0, 0)]
)
// into this JSON
{
    "Durations": [5, 3600, 0]
}
// and serializes
Foo::Bytes {
    bytes: vec![
        (1, vec![0, 1, 2]),
        (-100, vec![100, 200, 255]),
        (1, vec![0, 111, 222]),
    ],
}
// into this JSON
{
    "Bytes": {
        "bytes": {
            "1": "000102",
            "-100": "64c8ff",
            "1": "006fde"
        }
    }
}
```

# average - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/average/^0.16/

## Expand description

This crate provides estimators for statistics on a sequence of numbers. The typical workflow looks like this:

- If necessary, build your custom estimator using `concatenate``define_moments`
- Initialize the estimator of your choice with `new()`.
- Add some subset (called “sample”) of the sequence of numbers (called
“population”) for which you want to estimate the statistic, using `add()`or`collect()`.
- Calculate the statistic with `mean()`or similar.

You can run several estimators in parallel and merge them into one with
`merge()`.

Everything is calculated iteratively in a single pass using constant memory, so the sequence of numbers can be an iterator. The used algorithms try to avoid numerical instabilities.

If you want [Serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde) support,
include `"serde"` in your list of features.

Note that deserializing does not currently check for all invalid inputs.
For example, if you deserialize a corrupted [ Variance](https://docs.rs/struct.Variance.html) it may return
a negative value for variance, even though that is mathematically impossible.
In a future minor release some of these checks may be added.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use average::{MeanWithError, Estimate};
let mut a: MeanWithError = (1..6).map(f64::from).collect();
a.add(42.);
println!("The mean is {} ± {}.", a.mean(), a.error());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#estimators)Estimators

- Mean (`Mean``MeanWithError`
- Weighted mean (`WeightedMean``WeightedMeanWithError`
- Variance (`Variance``Skewness``Kurtosis`
- Arbitrary higher moments (`define_moments`
- Quantiles (`Quantile`
- Minimum (`Min``Max`

[§](https://docs.rs#estimating-several-statistics-at-once)Estimating several statistics at once

The estimators are designed to have minimal state. The recommended way to
calculate several of them at once is to create a struct with all the
estimators you need. You can then implement `add` for your struct by
forwarding to the underlying estimators. Everything is inlined, so there
should be no overhead.

You can avoid the boilerplate code by using the [ concatenate](https://docs.rs/macro.concatenate.html) macro.

Note that calculating moments requires calculating the lower moments, so you only need to include the highest moment in your struct.

[§](https://docs.rs#calculating-histograms)Calculating histograms

The [ define_histogram](https://docs.rs/macro.define_histogram.html) macro can be used to define a histogram struct that
uses constant memory. See

[(defined using](https://docs.rs/struct.Histogram10.html)

`Histogram10``define_histogram!(..., 10)`) and the extension trait [for the methods available to the generated struct.](https://docs.rs/trait.Histogram.html)

`Histogram`## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_almost_eq.html)- almost_ - eq
- Assert that two numbers are almost equal to each other.
- [concatenate](https://docs.rs/macro.concatenate.html)
- Concatenate several iterative estimators into one.
- [define_](https://docs.rs/macro.define_histogram.html)- histogram
- Define a histogram with a number of bins known at compile time.
- [define_](https://docs.rs/macro.define_moments.html)- moments
- Define an estimator of all moments up to a number given at compile time.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_extend.html)- extend
- Implement `Extend<f64>`for an iterative estimator.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_from_iterator.html)- from_ - iterator
- Implement `FromIterator<f64>`for an iterative estimator.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_from_par_iterator.html)- from_ - par_ - iterator
- Implement `FromParallelIterator<f64>`for an iterative estimator.

# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.10.0/

## Expand description

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of [PCG generators](https://www.pcg-random.org/).
The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in
other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

[§](https://docs.rs#generators)Generators

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`- `Lcg64Xsh32`- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`- `Lcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`- `Mcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

These generators are all deterministic and portable (see [Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html)
in the book), with testing against reference vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#seeding-construction)Seeding (construction)

Generators implement the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/seedable_rng/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait. All methods are suitable for
seeding. Some suggestions:

- To automatically seed with a unique seed, use `SeedableRng::from_rng``rand::rng()`
- Seed **from an integer**via`seed_from_u64`. This uses a hash function internally to yield a (typically) good seed from any input.`let rng = Pcg64Mcg::seed_from_u64(1);`

See also [Seeding RNGs](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-seeding.html) in the book.

[§](https://docs.rs#generation)Generation

Generators implement [ Rng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.Rng.html), whose methods may be used directly to
generate unbounded integer or byte values.

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, Rng};
use rand_pcg::Pcg64Mcg;
let mut rng = Pcg64Mcg::seed_from_u64(0);
let x = rng.next_u64();
assert_eq!(x, 0x5603f242407deca2);
```
It is often more convenient to use the [ rand::Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.rng.html) trait, which provides
further functionality. See also the

[Random Values](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-values.html)chapter in the book.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lcg64](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg64Xsh32.html)- Xsh32
- A PCG random number generator (XSH RR 64/32 (LCG) variant).
- [Lcg128](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg128CmDxsm64.html)- CmDxsm64
- A PCG random number generator (CM DXSM 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- [Lcg128](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg128Xsl64.html)- Xsl64
- A PCG random number generator (XSL RR 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- [Mcg128](https://docs.rs/struct.Mcg128Xsl64.html)- Xsl64
- A PCG random number generator (XSL 128/64 (MCG) variant).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Pcg32](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg32.html)
- `Lcg64Xsh32`- `pcg32`.
- [Pcg64](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg64.html)
- `Lcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64`.
- [Pcg64](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg64Dxsm.html)- Dxsm
- `Lcg128CmDxsm64`- `PCG64DXSM`.
- [Pcg64](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg64Mcg.html)- Mcg
- A friendly name for `Mcg128Xsl64``pcg64_fast`).

# rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/latest/target-redirect/rand_distr/

## Expand description

Generating random samples from probability distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-exports)Re-exports

This crate is a super-set of the [ rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html) module. See the

[module documentation for an overview of the core](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html)

`rand::distr`[trait and implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)

`Distribution`The following are re-exported:

- The `Distribution``Iter`
- The `StandardUniform``Alphanumeric``Uniform``OpenClosed01``Open01``Bernoulli`
- The `weighted`

[§](https://docs.rs#distributions)Distributions

This crate provides the following probability distributions:

- Related to real-valued quantities that grow linearly
(e.g. errors, offsets):
- `Normal`- `StandardNormal`
- `SkewNormal`
- `Cauchy`

- Related to Bernoulli trials (yes/no events, with a given probability):
- `Binomial`
- `Geometric`
- `Hypergeometric`

- Related to positive real-valued quantities that grow exponentially
(e.g. prices, incomes, populations):
- `LogNormal`

- Related to the occurrence of independent events at a given rate:
- Gamma and derived distributions:
- `Gamma`
- `ChiSquared`
- `StudentT`
- `FisherF`

- Triangular distribution:
- `Beta`
- `Triangular`

- Multivariate probability distributions
- `multi::Dirichlet`
- `UnitSphere`
- `UnitBall`
- `UnitCircle`
- `UnitDisc`

- Misc. distributions
- `InverseGaussian`
- `NormalInverseGaussian`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [num_traits](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/index.html);

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# rand::distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html

## Expand description

Generating random samples from probability distributions

This module is the home of the [ Distribution](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html) trait and several of its
implementations. It is the workhorse behind some of the convenient
functionality of the

[trait, e.g.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html)

`RngExt`[and of course](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.random)

`RngExt::random`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.sample)

`RngExt::sample`Abstractly, a [probability distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distribution) describes the probability of
occurrence of each value in its sample space.

More concretely, an implementation of `Distribution<T>` for type `X` is an
algorithm for choosing values from the sample space (a subset of `T`)
according to the distribution `X` represents, using an external source of
randomness (an RNG supplied to the `sample` function).

A type `X` may implement `Distribution<T>` for multiple types `T`.
Any type implementing [ Distribution](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html) is stateless (i.e. immutable),
but it may have internal parameters set at construction time (for example,

[allows specification of its sample space as a range within](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)

`Uniform``T`).[§](https://docs.rs#the-standard-uniform-distribution)The Standard Uniform distribution

The [ StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html) distribution is important to mention. This is the
distribution used by

[and represents the “default” way to produce a random value for many different types, including most primitive types, tuples, arrays, and a few derived types. See the documentation of](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.random)

`RngExt::random`[for more details.](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html)

`StandardUniform`Implementing [ Distribution<T>](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html) for

[for user types](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html)

`StandardUniform``T` makes it
possible to generate type `T` with [, and by extension also with the](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.random)

`RngExt::random`[function.](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)

`random`[§](https://docs.rs#other-standard-uniform-distributions)Other standard uniform distributions

[ Alphanumeric](https://docs.rs/struct.Alphanumeric.html) is a simple distribution to sample random letters and
numbers of the

`char` type; in contrast [may sample any valid](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html)

`StandardUniform``char`.There’s also an [ Alphabetic](https://docs.rs/struct.Alphabetic.html) distribution which acts similarly to

[but doesn’t include digits.](https://docs.rs/struct.Alphanumeric.html)

`Alphanumeric`For floats (`f32`, `f64`), [ StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html) samples from

`[0, 1)`. Also
provided are [(samples from](https://docs.rs/struct.Open01.html)

`Open01``(0, 1)`) and [(samples from](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenClosed01.html)

`OpenClosed01``(0, 1]`). No option is provided to sample from `[0, 1]`; it
is suggested to use one of the above half-open ranges since the failure to
sample a value which would have a low chance of being sampled anyway is
rarely an issue in practice.[§](https://docs.rs#parameterized-uniform-distributions)Parameterized Uniform distributions

The [ Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html) distribution provides uniform sampling over a specified
range on a subset of the types supported by the above distributions.

Implementations support single-value-sampling via
[ Rng::random_range(Range)](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.random_range).
Where a fixed (non-

`const`) range will be sampled many times, it is likely
faster to pre-construct a [object using](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)

`Distribution`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html#method.new)

`Uniform::new`[or](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html#method.new_inclusive)

`Uniform::new_inclusive``From<Range>`.[§](https://docs.rs#non-uniform-sampling)Non-uniform sampling

Sampling a simple true/false outcome with a given probability has a name:
the [ Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/struct.Bernoulli.html) distribution (this is used by

[).](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html#method.random_bool)

`RngExt::random_bool`For weighted sampling of discrete values see the [ weighted](https://docs.rs/weighted/index.html) module.

This crate no longer includes other non-uniform distributions; instead
it is recommended that you use either [ rand_distr](https://crates.io/crates/rand_distr) or

[.](https://crates.io/crates/statrs)

`statrs`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [slice](https://docs.rs/slice/index.html)
- Distributions over slices
- [uniform](https://docs.rs/uniform/index.html)
- A distribution uniformly sampling numbers within a given range.
- [weighted](https://docs.rs/weighted/index.html)- `alloc`
- Weighted (index) sampling

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Alphabetic](https://docs.rs/struct.Alphabetic.html)
- Sample a `u8`
- [Alphanumeric](https://docs.rs/struct.Alphanumeric.html)
- Sample a `u8`, uniformly distributed over ASCII letters and numbers: a-z, A-Z and 0-9.
- [Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/struct.Bernoulli.html)
- The [Bernoulli distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_distribution)`Bernoulli(p)`.
- [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)
- An iterator over a `Distribution`
- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- A `Distribution``S`
- [Open01](https://docs.rs/struct.Open01.html)
- A distribution to sample floating point numbers uniformly in the open
interval `(0, 1)`, i.e. not including either endpoint.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenClosed01.html)- Closed01
- A distribution to sample floating point numbers uniformly in the half-open
interval `(0, 1]`, i.e. including 1 but not 0.
- [Standard](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html)- Uniform
- The Standard Uniform distribution
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)
- Sample values uniformly between two bounds.

# synth-verify - Formal Verification for Synth Compiler

Formal verification infrastructure for the Synth WebAssembly-to-ARM compiler using SMT-based translation validation.

## Overview

This crate provides:

- **SMT-based translation validation**using Z3 SMT solver
- **Formal semantics**for WebAssembly and ARM operations
- **Property-based testing**framework with proptest
- **Automated verification**of synthesis rules

## Architecture

```
synth-verify/
├── wasm_semantics.rs      # WASM → SMT encoding (25+ operations)
├── arm_semantics.rs       # ARM → SMT encoding (processor state model)
├── translation_validator.rs # Equivalence prover (Alive2-inspired)
└── properties.rs          # Property-based tests (50+ properties)
```
## Usage

### Verifying a Synthesis Rule

```
use ;
use ;
// Create Z3 context
let ctx = create_z3_context;
let validator = new;
// Define a synthesis rule
let rule = SynthesisRule ;
// Verify the rule
match validator.verify_rule
```
### Batch Verification

```
// Verify multiple rules
let rules = vec!;
let results = validator.verify_rules;
for  in results
```
### Property-Based Testing

```
use CompilerProperties;
use *;
proptest!
```
## Verification Approach

### Translation Validation

For each synthesis rule `WASM_OP → ARM_OPS`, we prove:

```
∀inputs. ⟦WASM_OP⟧(inputs) = ⟦ARM_OPS⟧(inputs)
```
Using SMT solver:

- Create symbolic inputs
- Encode WASM semantics: `φ_wasm`
- Encode ARM semantics: `φ_arm`
- Assert: `φ_wasm ≠ φ_arm`
- Check satisfiability:
- **UNSAT**→ Proven correct
- **SAT**→ Counterexample found
- **UNKNOWN**→ Timeout

### Example: ADD Verification

```
; Symbolic inputs
(declare-const a (_ BitVec 32))
(declare-const b (_ BitVec 32))
; WASM: i32.add
(define-fun wasm-add () (_ BitVec 32)
  (bvadd a b))
; ARM: ADD R0, R0, R1
(define-fun arm-add () (_ BitVec 32)
  (bvadd a b))
; Prove equivalence
(assert (not (= wasm-add arm-add)))
(check-sat)  ; Returns: unsat → Proven!
```
## Verified Operations

| Operation | Status | Method |
|---|---|---|
| i32.add | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.sub | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.mul | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.div_s | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.div_u | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.and | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.or | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.xor | ✓ Proven | SMT |
| i32.shl | ⚠ Partial | Complex |
| i32.shr_u | ⚠ Partial | Complex |
| i32.shr_s | ⚠ Partial | Complex |

## Dependencies

### Required

- **z3**- Z3 SMT solver Rust bindings (v0.12)
- **synth-synthesis**- Synthesis rules and operations
- **proptest**- Property-based testing

### System Requirements

Z3 requires either:

- System installation: `libz3-dev`or`z3`package
- Static linking: Built automatically (requires C++ compiler)

For development without Z3:

```
# Skip tests that require Z3
```
## Testing

```
# Run all tests (requires Z3)
# Run specific test suites
# Property-based testing with more cases
PROPTEST_CASES=10000
```
## Performance

- Verification time: 50-500ms per rule (SMT solving)
- Memory usage: ~50MB (Z3 context)
- Scalability: Linear in number of rules

## Limitations

- **Shift operations**: Modulo handling complex for SMT
- **Control flow**: Branch verification requires extended modeling
- **Memory operations**: Requires memory model formalization
- **Floating point**: Not yet supported

## Future Work

### Phase 1: Complete SMT Coverage

- Shift operation verification
- Control flow (branches, conditions)
- Memory operations (load/store)

### Phase 2: Optimization Verification

- DCE, constant folding, CSE correctness
- Loop optimization soundness
- Register allocation preservation

### Phase 3: Mechanized Proofs

- Port to Coq proof assistant
- Machine-checked correctness
- Certified synthesis rule library

## References

- **Alive2**: Automated LLVM verification (Lopes et al., PLDI 2021)
- **CompCert**: Verified C compiler (Leroy, POPL 2006)
- **VeriISLE**: Verified instruction selection (Nandi et al., PLDI 2020)
- **Z3**: Efficient SMT solver (de Moura & Bjørner, TACAS 2008)

Dual-licensed under Apache-2.0 OR MIT

## Authors

PulseEngine Team

# oxen-cli 0.51.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/oxen-cli/0.51.1

# oxen-cli

The client for interacting with `oxen` repositories, both locally and remote.

## Build

See the [prerequisites](https://docs.rs/README.md#prerequisites) section of the main readme before developing.
Use the standard `cargo ... --workspace` commands and `cargo ... -p oxen-cli` commands.

## Run

Initialize a new repository or clone an existing one:

```
```
This will create the `.oxen` dir in your current directory and allow you to run Oxen CLI commands:

```
```
## Logging

Oxen uses structured logging.
It outputs to STDERR by default but can be configured with rotating log files.
See [Logging](https://docs.rs/README.md#logging) for details.

By default, the `oxen` CLI does not perform any logging. Set `RUST_LOG` to change.

## OpenTelemetry Tracing

The `oxen` CLI can export tracing spans to any OTLP-compatible collector
(Jaeger, Tempo, etc.). This requires building with the `otel` feature flag:

```
```
At runtime, set **both** `OXEN_OTEL_ENDPOINT` and `RUST_LOG=info`:

```
OXEN_OTEL_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317 RUST_LOG=info
```
### Why `RUST_LOG=info` is required

The CLI defaults to `LevelFilter::OFF` when `RUST_LOG` is not set. The
`RUST_LOG` filter is global — it gates what reaches **all** tracing outputs,
including the OpenTelemetry exporter. Since `#[tracing::instrument]` creates
spans at `INFO` level, they are silently dropped before the OTel layer ever
sees them unless the filter is at `INFO` or below.

Setting `OXEN_OTEL_ENDPOINT` alone is not enough — you must also set
`RUST_LOG=info` (or more targeted, e.g. `RUST_LOG=liboxen=info`) for spans
to be exported.

| Variable | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `OXEN_OTEL_ENDPOINT` | Collector endpoint URL. Absent = disabled. | (none) |
| `OXEN_OTEL_PROTOCOL` | Transport: `grpc`or`http` | `grpc` |
| `RUST_LOG` | Must include `info`level for spans to be exported | `off` |

### Quick start with Jaeger

```
# Start Jaeger all-in-one: https://www.jaegertracing.io/docs/2.17/
# Run a pull with tracing enabled
OXEN_OTEL_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317 RUST_LOG=info
# View traces at http://localhost:16686 under service "oxen"
```
When the `otel` feature is not compiled in, no OpenTelemetry dependencies
are included and the env vars are ignored.

# delta_explain - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/delta-explain/0.3.0/delta_explain/

## Expand description

delta-explain: make Delta Lake file pruning visible.

This library crate hosts the analysis machinery behind the `delta-explain`
CLI: predicate classification and lowering, kernel-backed scanning and
statistics, and report rendering. The binary in `main.rs` is the CLI layer
on top.

**API stability**: the Rust API is currently internal and unstable. It
exists to serve the CLI and its tests; module structure and signatures may
change between releases without semver guarantees. The CLI surface and the
versioned JSON output schema are the stable contracts.

how it is shown. Rendering (text and JSON) lives in `crate::render`

# smos - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smos/0.3.4/smos/

## Expand description

`smos` — concrete implementations of the application-layer ports.

This crate is the *only* place IO happens in the SMOS Rust port. Each
adapter implements a `smos_application::ports` trait against a specific
external system (SurrealDB for persistence, system clock for time, HTTP
for LLM upstream, OpenAI-compatible `llama-server` endpoints for
embeddings/extraction/rerank, ort + ONNX Runtime for NLI).

See `smos-poc/ТРЕБОВАНИЯ.md` for the canonical specification and
`smos-application` for the port shapes.

# synth_backend_riscv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-backend-riscv/0.24.0/synth_backend_riscv/

## Expand description

RISC-V backend for synth — RV32IMAC encoder, ELF builder, PMP allocator.

Mirrors the structure of `synth-backend` (ARM Cortex-M) but emits RISC-V
machine code. The instruction selector lives in `synth-synthesis::riscv`;
this crate contains the binary encoder, ELF emission, linker script
generation, and Physical Memory Protection (PMP) allocator.

Supported variants (per `TargetSpec::IsaVariant::RiscV32 { extensions }`):

- RV32I — base 32-bit integer
- RV32IM — adds multiply/divide
- RV32IMA — adds atomics
- RV32IMAC — adds compressed (16-bit) instructions

The encoder always emits 32-bit instructions in this skeleton. The 16-bit C-extension encoding will be a peephole pass in a follow-up.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [RiscVBackend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.RiscVBackend.html);
- `pub use elf_builder::`- [ElfMode](https://docs.rs/elf_builder/enum.ElfMode.html);

# synth_backend - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-backend/0.24.0/synth_backend/

## Expand description

Synth Backend - Code generation and binary emission

Generic scaffolding (ELF builder, linker scripts, memory layout) is always
available. ARM-specific modules are behind the `arm-cortex-m` feature.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use elf_builder::`- [ArmRelocationType](https://docs.rs/elf_builder/enum.ArmRelocationType.html);

# agnix-mcp 0.37.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/agnix-mcp/0.37.0

agnix-mcp-0.37.0 is not a library.

                MCP server for agnix - AI agent config linter

Exposes agnix validation as MCP tools for AI assistants.

## MCP Best Practices Implemented

- **Clear tool descriptions**: Each tool has a detailed description explaining what it does, when to use it, and what it returns
- **Rich parameter schemas**: All parameters have descriptions with examples
- **Structured outputs**: Returns JSON with predictable schema for easy parsing
- **Error handling**: Proper error messages with context
- **Server metadata**: Provides name, version, and usage instructions

# synth_backend_aarch64 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/synth-backend-aarch64/0.24.0/synth_backend_aarch64/

## Expand description

AArch64 (A64) host-native backend for synth — **milestone 1** (#538).

Goal (from #538): a minimal A64 integer-subset backend reachable via
`-b aarch64`, so synth output runs and debugs natively on arm64 dev hosts
(Apple Silicon, arm64 Linux/CI) instead of only under QEMU/Renode — and so a
third backend becomes a third differential oracle against the Thumb-2 and RV32
lowerings.

[§](https://docs.rs#milestone-status)Milestone status

- **1a (this crate, now):**the verified A64- *encoder*(integer data-processing +- `movz`/- `movk`+- `ret`, cross-checked against- `clang`) and a minimal straight-line- *selector*(params in- `w0..w7`, i32 add/sub/mul/and/or/xor + const, result to- `w0`,- `ret`).- `compile_bytes`turns a leaf integer function’s wasm ops into A64 machine code. Ops outside the subset return- `Unsupported`— an honest loud-skip, never wrong code.
- **1b (next):**an- `EM_AARCH64`relocatable-ELF emitter, the- `Backend`trait impl,- `-b aarch64`CLI wiring, and the native differential-execution acceptance probe (- `synth compile add.wat -b aarch64`→ link + run on the arm64 host, diff vs wasmtime).
- **later:**spilling, i64, floats, memory, control flow, calls, DWARF.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use backend::`- [AArch64Backend](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.AArch64Backend.html);
- `pub use selector::`- [SelectError](https://docs.rs/selector/struct.SelectError.html);
- `pub use selector::`- [select](https://docs.rs/selector/fn.select.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- `Backend`trait implementation for the AArch64 host-native backend (#538).
- [elf](https://docs.rs/elf/index.html)
- Minimal `EM_AARCH64`ELF64 relocatable-object emitter — milestone-1b (#538).
- [encoder](https://docs.rs/encoder/index.html)
- Minimal AArch64 (A64) instruction encoder — milestone-1 integer subset (#538).
- [selector](https://docs.rs/selector/index.html)
- Minimal AArch64 instruction selector — milestone-1 integer subset (#538).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [compile_](https://docs.rs/fn.compile_bytes.html)- bytes
- Lower a single leaf integer function (wasm ops + declared param count) to A64
machine-code bytes (little-endian 32-bit words). Convenience over
`selector::select``.text`bytes.

# rand_distr 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/0.6.0

# rand_distr

Implements a full suite of random number distribution sampling routines.

This crate is a superset of the [rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/distr/index.html) module, including support
for sampling from Beta, Binomial, Cauchy, ChiSquared, Dirichlet, Exponential,
FisherF, Gamma, Geometric, Hypergeometric, InverseGaussian, LogNormal, Normal,
Pareto, PERT, Poisson, StudentT, Triangular and Weibull distributions.  Sampling
from the unit ball, unit circle, unit disc and unit sphere surfaces is also
supported.

It is worth mentioning the [statrs](https://github.com/statrs-dev/statrs) crate which provides similar functionality
along with various support functions, including PDF and CDF computation. In
contrast, this `rand_distr` crate focuses on sampling from distributions.

## Portability and libm

The floating point functions from `num_traits` and `libm` are used to support
`no_std` environments and ensure reproducibility. If the floating point
functions from `std` are preferred, which may provide better accuracy and
performance but may produce different random values, the `std_math` feature
can be enabled. (Note that any other crate depending on `num-traits` with the
`std` feature (default-enabled) will have the same effect.)

## Crate features

- `std`(enabled by default):- `rand_distr`implements the- `Error`trait for its error types. Implies- `alloc`and- `rand/std`.
- `alloc`(enabled by default): required for some distributions when not using- `std`(in particular,- `Dirichlet`and- `WeightedAliasIndex`).
- `std_math`: see above on portability and libm
- `serde`: implement (de)seriaialization using- `serde`

## Links

## Old Issues and Pull Requests

- All closed Issues and merged Pull requests from before 5.February.2025 (version 0.5.0) can be found in the [rand](https://github.com/rust-random/rand)repository where this crate used to be.

## License

`rand_distr` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/0.6.0/target-redirect/rand_distr/

## Expand description

Generating random samples from probability distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-exports)Re-exports

This crate is a super-set of the [ rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html) module. See the

[module documentation for an overview of the core](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html)

`rand::distr`[trait and implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)

`Distribution`The following are re-exported:

- The `Distribution``Iter`
- The `StandardUniform``Alphanumeric``Uniform``OpenClosed01``Open01``Bernoulli`
- The `weighted`

[§](https://docs.rs#distributions)Distributions

This crate provides the following probability distributions:

- Related to real-valued quantities that grow linearly
(e.g. errors, offsets):
- `Normal`- `StandardNormal`
- `SkewNormal`
- `Cauchy`

- Related to Bernoulli trials (yes/no events, with a given probability):
- `Binomial`
- `Geometric`
- `Hypergeometric`

- Related to positive real-valued quantities that grow exponentially
(e.g. prices, incomes, populations):
- `LogNormal`

- Related to the occurrence of independent events at a given rate:
- Gamma and derived distributions:
- `Gamma`
- `ChiSquared`
- `StudentT`
- `FisherF`

- Triangular distribution:
- `Beta`
- `Triangular`

- Multivariate probability distributions
- `multi::Dirichlet`
- `UnitSphere`
- `UnitBall`
- `UnitCircle`
- `UnitDisc`

- Misc. distributions
- `InverseGaussian`
- `NormalInverseGaussian`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [num_traits](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [multi](https://docs.rs/multi/index.html)
- Contains Multi-dimensional distributions.
- [uniform](https://docs.rs/uniform/index.html)
- A distribution uniformly sampling numbers within a given range.
- [weighted](https://docs.rs/weighted/index.html)
- Weighted (index) sampling

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Alphanumeric](https://docs.rs/struct.Alphanumeric.html)

# rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/index.html

## Expand description

Generating random samples from probability distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-exports)Re-exports

This crate is a super-set of the [ rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html) module. See the

[module documentation for an overview of the core](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html)

`rand::distr`[trait and implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)

`Distribution`The following are re-exported:

- The `Distribution``Iter`
- The `StandardUniform``Alphanumeric``Uniform``OpenClosed01``Open01``Bernoulli`
- The `weighted`

[§](https://docs.rs#distributions)Distributions

This crate provides the following probability distributions:

- Related to real-valued quantities that grow linearly
(e.g. errors, offsets):
- `Normal`- `StandardNormal`
- `SkewNormal`
- `Cauchy`

- Related to Bernoulli trials (yes/no events, with a given probability):
- `Binomial`
- `Geometric`
- `Hypergeometric`

- Related to positive real-valued quantities that grow exponentially
(e.g. prices, incomes, populations):
- `LogNormal`

- Related to the occurrence of independent events at a given rate:
- Gamma and derived distributions:
- `Gamma`
- `ChiSquared`
- `StudentT`
- `FisherF`

- Triangular distribution:
- `Beta`
- `Triangular`

- Multivariate probability distributions
- `multi::Dirichlet`
- `UnitSphere`
- `UnitBall`
- `UnitCircle`
- `UnitDisc`

- Misc. distributions
- `InverseGaussian`
- `NormalInverseGaussian`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [num_traits](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [multi](https://docs.rs/multi/index.html)
- Contains Multi-dimensional distributions.
- [uniform](https://docs.rs/uniform/index.html)
- A distribution uniformly sampling numbers within a given range.
- [weighted](https://docs.rs/weighted/index.html)
- Weighted (index) sampling

[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! Generating random samples from probability distributions.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! ## Re-exports
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! This crate is a super-set of the [`rand::distr`] module. See the
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! [`rand::distr`] module documentation for an overview of the core
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! [`Distribution`] trait and implementations.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! The following are re-exported:
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! - The [`Distribution`] trait and [`Iter`] helper type
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! - The [`StandardUniform`], [`Alphanumeric`], [`Uniform`], [`OpenClosed01`],
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!   [`Open01`], [`Bernoulli`] distributions
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! - The [`weighted`] module
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! ## Distributions
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! This crate provides the following probability distributions:
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! - Related to real-valued quantities that grow linearly
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!   (e.g. errors, offsets):
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!   - [`Normal`] distribution, and [`StandardNormal`] as a primitive
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!   - [`SkewNormal`] distribution
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!   - [`Cauchy`] distribution
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! - Related to Bernoulli trials (yes/no events, with a given probability):
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!   - [`Binomial`] distribution
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!   - [`Geometric`] distribution
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!   - [`Hypergeometric`] distribution
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! - Related to positive real-valued quantities that grow exponentially
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!   (e.g. prices, incomes, populations):
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!   - [`LogNormal`] distribution
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! - Related to the occurrence of independent events at a given rate:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!   - [`Pareto`] distribution
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!   - [`Poisson`] distribution
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!   - [`Exp`]onential distribution, and [`Exp1`] as a primitive
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!   - [`Weibull`] distribution
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!   - [`Gumbel`] distribution
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!   - [`Frechet`] distribution
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!   - [`Zeta`] distribution
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!   - [`Zipf`] distribution
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! - Gamma and derived distributions:
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!   - [`Gamma`] distribution
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!   - [`ChiSquared`] distribution
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!   - [`StudentT`] distribution
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!   - [`FisherF`] distribution
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! - Triangular distribution:
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!   - [`Beta`] distribution
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!   - [`Triangular`] distribution
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! - Multivariate probability distributions
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!   - [`multi::Dirichlet`] distribution
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!   - [`UnitSphere`] distribution
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!   - [`UnitBall`] distribution
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!   - [`UnitCircle`] distribution
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!   - [`UnitDisc`] distribution
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! - Misc. distributions
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!   - [`InverseGaussian`] distribution
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!   - [`NormalInverseGaussian`] distribution

[136](https://docs.rs#136)mod test {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    // Notes on testing
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    //
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    // Testing random number distributions correctly is hard. The following
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    // testing is desired:
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    //
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    // - Construction: test initialisation with a few valid parameter sets.
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    // - Erroneous usage: test that incorrect usage generates an error.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    // - Vector: test that usage with fixed inputs (including RNG) generates a
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    //   fixed output sequence on all platforms.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    // - Correctness at fixed points (optional): using a specific mock RNG,
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    //   check that specific values are sampled (e.g. end-points and median of
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    //   distribution).
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    // - Correctness of PDF (extra): generate a histogram of samples within a
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    //   certain range, and check this approximates the PDF. These tests are
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    //   expected to be expensive, and should be behind a feature-gate.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)    //
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    // TODO: Vector and correctness tests are largely absent so far.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    // NOTE: Some distributions have tests checking only that samples can be
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    // generated. This is redundant with vector and correctness tests.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// An RNG which panics on first use
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    pub struct VoidRng;
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    impl rand::TryRng for VoidRng {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        type Error = rand::rand_core::Infallible;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)        fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Self::Error> {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            panic!("usage of VoidRng")
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        }
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Self::Error> {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)            panic!("usage of VoidRng")
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        }
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, _: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            panic!("usage of VoidRng")
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    }
[171](https://docs.rs#171)
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// Construct a deterministic RNG with the given seed
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    pub fn rng(seed: u64) -> impl rand::RngExt {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        // For tests, we want a statistically good, fast, reproducible RNG.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        // PCG32 will do fine, and will be easy to embed if we ever need to.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        const INC: u64 = 11634580027462260723;
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        rand_pcg::Pcg32::new(seed, INC)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// Assert that two numbers are almost equal to each other.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    ///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// On panic, this macro will print the values of the expressions with their
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// debug representations.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    macro_rules! assert_almost_eq {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        ($a:expr, $b:expr, $prec:expr) => {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            let diff = ($a - $b).abs();
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            assert!(
[188](https://docs.rs#188)                diff <= $prec,
[189](https://docs.rs#189)                "assertion failed: `abs(left - right) = {:.1e} < {:e}`, \
[190](https://docs.rs#190)                    (left: `{}`, right: `{}`)",
[191](https://docs.rs#191)                diff,
[192](https://docs.rs#192)                $prec,
[193](https://docs.rs#193)                $a,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)                $b
[195](https://docs.rs#195)            );
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        };
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    }

# Distribution in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/trait.Distribution.html

```
pub trait Distribution<T> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[sample](https://docs.rs#tymethod.sample)<R>(&self, rng: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> T
       where R: [Rng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.Rng.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html);
    // Provided methods
    fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<R>(self, rng: R) -> [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)<Self, R, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)
       where R: [Rng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.Rng.html),
             Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[map](https://docs.rs#method.map)<F, S>(self, func: F) -> [Map](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/distribution/struct.Map.html)<Self, F, T, S>
       where F: [Fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.Fn.html)(T) -> S,
             Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

Types (distributions) that can be used to create a random instance of `T`.

It is possible to sample from a distribution through both the
`Distribution` and [`RngExt`] traits, via `distr.sample(&mut rng)` and
`rng.sample(distr)`. They also both offer the [ sample_iter](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html#method.sample_iter) method, which
produces an iterator that samples from the distribution.

All implementations are expected to be immutable; this has the significant advantage of not needing to consider thread safety, and for most distributions efficient state-less sampling algorithms are available.

Implementations are typically expected to be portable with reproducible
results when used with a PRNG with fixed seed; see the
[portability chapter](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
of The Rust Rand Book. In some cases this does not apply, e.g. the `usize`
type requires different sampling on 32-bit and 64-bit machines.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/distribution.rs.html#75-78)#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<R>(self, rng: R) -> [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)<Self, R, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/distribution.rs.html#75-78)

#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<R>(self, rng: R) -> [Iter](https://docs.rs/struct.Iter.html)<Self, R, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Create an iterator that generates random values of `T`, using `rng` as
the source of randomness.

Note that this function takes `self` by value. This works since
`Distribution<T>` is impl’d for `&D` where `D: Distribution<T>`,
however borrowing is not automatic hence `distr.sample_iter(...)` may
need to be replaced with `(&distr).sample_iter(...)` to borrow or
`(&*distr).sample_iter(...)` to reborrow an existing reference.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::distr::{Distribution, Alphanumeric, Uniform, StandardUniform};
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Vec of 16 x f32:
let v: Vec<f32> = StandardUniform.sample_iter(&mut rng).take(16).collect();
// String:
let s: String = Alphanumeric
    .sample_iter(&mut rng)
    .take(7)
    .map(char::from)
    .collect();
// Dice-rolling:
let die_range = Uniform::new_inclusive(1, 6).unwrap();
let mut roll_die = die_range.sample_iter(&mut rng);
while roll_die.next().unwrap() != 6 {
    println!("Not a 6; rolling again!");
}
```
Map sampled values to type `S`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use rand::distr::{Distribution, Uniform};
let die = Uniform::new_inclusive(1, 6).unwrap();
let even_number = die.map(|num| num % 2 == 0);
while !even_number.sample(&mut rand::rng()) {
    println!("Still odd; rolling again!");
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

Caution: This method panics if there are no elements or all weights are zero. However,

Struct Iter  Copy item path  Source  `pub struct Iter<D, R, T> {  }`Expand description An iterator over a `Distribution`

This iterator yields random values of type `T` with distribution `D`
from a random generator of type `R`.

Construct this `struct` using `Distribution::sample_iter``RngExt::sample_iter`]. It is also used by [`RngExt::random_iter`] and
[`crate::random_iter`].

Formats the value using the given formatter.

# StandardUniform in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.StandardUniform.html

`pub struct StandardUniform;`## Expand description

The Standard Uniform distribution

This [ Distribution](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html) is the

*standard*parameterization of

[. Bounds are selected according to the output type.](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)

`Uniform`Assuming the provided `Rng` is well-behaved, these implementations
generate values with the following ranges and distributions:

- Integers (`i8`,`i32`,`u64`, etc.) are uniformly distributed over the whole range of the type (thus each possible value may be sampled with equal probability).
- `char`is uniformly distributed over all Unicode scalar values, i.e. all code points in the range- `0...0x10_FFFF`, except for the range- `0xD800...0xDFFF`(the surrogate code points). This includes unassigned/reserved code points. For some uses, the- `Alphanumeric`- `Alphabetic`
- `bool`samples- `false`or- `true`, each with probability 0.5.
- Floating point types (`f32`and`f64`) are uniformly distributed in the half-open range`[0, 1)`. See also the[notes below](https://docs.rs#floating-point-implementation).
- Wrapping integers (`Wrapping<T>`
- Non-zero integers (`NonZeroU8`

The `StandardUniform` distribution also supports generation of the following
compound types where all component types are supported:

- Tuples (up to 12 elements): each element is sampled sequentially and independently (thus, assuming a well-behaved RNG, there is no correlation between elements).
- Arrays `[T; n]`where`T`is supported. Each element is sampled sequentially and independently. Note that for small`T`this usually results in the RNG discarding random bits; see also`RngExt::fill`
- SIMD types (requires `simd_support``__m128i``std::simd`’s`u32x4``f32x4``mask32x4`

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-implementations)Custom implementations

The [ StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html) distribution may be implemented for user types as follows:

```
use rand::{Rng, RngExt};
use rand::distr::{Distribution, StandardUniform};
struct MyF32 {
    x: f32,
}
impl Distribution<MyF32> for StandardUniform {
    fn sample<R: Rng + ?Sized>(&self, rng: &mut R) -> MyF32 {
        MyF32 { x: rng.random() }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-usage)Example usage

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand::distr::StandardUniform;
let val: f32 = rand::rng().sample(StandardUniform);
println!("f32 from [0, 1): {}", val);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#floating-point-implementation)Floating point implementation

The floating point implementations for `StandardUniform` generate a random value in
the half-open interval `[0, 1)`, i.e. including 0 but not 1.

All values that can be generated are of the form `n * ε/2`. For `f32`
the 24 most significant random bits of a `u32` are used and for `f64` the
53 most significant bits of a `u64` are used. The conversion uses the
multiplicative method: `(rng.gen::<$uty>() >> N) as $ty * (ε/2)`.

See also: [ Open01](https://docs.rs/struct.Open01.html) which samples from

`(0, 1)`, [which samples from](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenClosed01.html)

`OpenClosed01``(0, 1]` and `Rng::random_range(0..1)` which also samples from
`[0, 1)`. Note that `Open01` uses transmute-based methods which yield 1 bit
less precision but may perform faster on some architectures (on modern Intel
CPUs all methods have approximately equal performance).## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)
