# Alphanumeric in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Alphanumeric.html

`pub struct Alphanumeric;`## Expand description

Sample a `u8`, uniformly distributed over ASCII letters and numbers:
a-z, A-Z and 0-9.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::RngExt;
use rand::distr::Alphanumeric;
let mut rng = rand::rng();
let chars: String = (0..7).map(|_| rng.sample(Alphanumeric) as char).collect();
println!("Random chars: {}", chars);
```
The [ SampleString](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/distribution/trait.SampleString.html) trait provides an easier method of generating
a random

[, and offers more efficient allocation:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`String````
use rand::distr::{Alphanumeric, SampleString};
let string = Alphanumeric.sample_string(&mut rand::rng(), 16);
println!("Random string: {}", string);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#passwords)Passwords

Users sometimes ask whether it is safe to use a string of random characters
as a password. In principle, all RNGs in Rand implementing `CryptoRng` are
suitable as a source of randomness for generating passwords (if they are
properly seeded), but it is more conservative to only use randomness
directly from the operating system via the `getrandom` crate, or the
corresponding bindings of a crypto library.

When generating passwords or keys, it is important to consider the threat model and in some cases the memorability of the password. This is out of scope of the Rand project, and therefore we defer to the following references:

# Uniform in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Uniform.html

```
pub struct Uniform<X>(/* private fields */)
where
    X:
```
[SampleUniform](https://docs.rs/uniform/trait.SampleUniform.html);## Expand description

Sample values uniformly between two bounds.

[§](https://docs.rs#construction)Construction

[ Uniform::new](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html#method.new) and

[construct a uniform distribution sampling from the given](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html#method.new_inclusive)

`Uniform::new_inclusive``low` and `high` limits. `Uniform` may
also be constructed via [as in](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html)

`TryFrom``Uniform::try_from(1..=6).unwrap()`.Constructors may do extra work up front to allow faster sampling of multiple
values. Where only a single sample is required it is suggested to use
[ Rng::random_range](RngExt::random_range) or one of the

`sample_single` methods instead.When sampling from a constant range, many calculations can happen at
compile-time and all methods should be fast; for floating-point ranges and
the full range of integer types, this should have comparable performance to
the [ StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided implementations

- `char`(- `UniformChar`- `u32`
- `f32`,- `f64`(- `UniformFloat`
- Integer types (`UniformInt``2^n`samples where n is 56 (`i8`and`u8`), 48 (`i16`and`u16`), 96 (`i32`and`u32`), 64 (`i64`and`u64`), 128 (`i128`and`u128`). The`unbiased`feature flag fixes this bias.
- `usize`(- `UniformUsize`- `u32`implementation where possible to enable portable results across 32-bit and 64-bit CPU architectures.
- `Duration`(- `UniformDuration`- `u32`or- `u64`
- SIMD types (requires `simd_support``__m128i``std::simd`’s`u32x4``f32x4``mask32x4`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::distr::{Distribution, Uniform};
let between = Uniform::try_from(10..10000).unwrap();
let mut rng = rand::rng();
let mut sum = 0;
for _ in 0..1000 {
    sum += between.sample(&mut rng);
}
println!("{}", sum);
```
For a single sample, [ Rng::random_range](RngExt::random_range) may be preferred:

```
use rand::RngExt;
let mut rng = rand::rng();
println!("{}", rng.random_range(0..10));
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new `Uniform` instance, which samples uniformly from the half
open range `[low, high)` (excluding `high`).

For discrete types (e.g. integers), samples will always be strictly less
than `high`. For (approximations of) continuous types (e.g. `f32`, `f64`),
samples may equal `high` due to loss of precision but may not be
greater than `high`.

Fails if `low >= high`, or if `low`, `high` or the range `high - low` is
non-finite. In release mode, only the range is checked.

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/uniform.rs.html#248-251)#### pub fn [new_inclusive](https://docs.rs#method.new_inclusive)<B1, B2>(low: B1, high: B2) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)<X>, [Error](https://docs.rs/uniform/enum.Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/uniform.rs.html#248-251)

#### pub fn [new_inclusive](https://docs.rs#method.new_inclusive)<B1, B2>(low: B1, high: B2) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)<X>, [Error](https://docs.rs/uniform/enum.Error.html)>

Create a new `Uniform` instance, which samples uniformly from the closed
range `[low, high]` (inclusive).

Fails if `low > high`, or if `low`, `high` or the range `high - low` is
non-finite. In release mode, only the range is checked.

# OpenClosed01 in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.OpenClosed01.html

`pub struct OpenClosed01;`## Expand description

A distribution to sample floating point numbers uniformly in the half-open
interval `(0, 1]`, i.e. including 1 but not 0.

All values that can be generated are of the form `n * ε/2`. For `f32`
the 24 most significant random bits of a `u32` are used and for `f64` the
53 most significant bits of a `u64` are used. The conversion uses the
multiplicative method.

See also: [ StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html) which samples from

`[0, 1)`, [which samples from](https://docs.rs/struct.Open01.html)

`Open01``(0, 1)` and [which samples from arbitrary ranges.](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)

`Uniform`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::RngExt;
use rand::distr::OpenClosed01;
let val: f32 = rand::rng().sample(OpenClosed01);
println!("f32 from (0, 1): {}", val);
```
## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/float.rs.html#45)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-OpenClosed01)

### impl [Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) for [OpenClosed01](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenClosed01.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/float.rs.html#46)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Deserialize%3C'de%3E-for-OpenClosed01)### impl<'de> [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> for [OpenClosed01](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenClosed01.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/float.rs.html#46)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Deserialize%3C'de%3E-for-OpenClosed01)

# Open01 in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Open01.html

`pub struct Open01;`## Expand description

A distribution to sample floating point numbers uniformly in the open
interval `(0, 1)`, i.e. not including either endpoint.

All values that can be generated are of the form `n * ε + ε/2`. For `f32`
the 23 most significant random bits of an `u32` are used, for `f64` 52 from
an `u64`. The conversion uses a transmute-based method.

See also: [ StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html) which samples from

`[0, 1)`, [which samples from](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenClosed01.html)

`OpenClosed01``(0, 1]` and [which samples from arbitrary ranges.](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)

`Uniform`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::RngExt;
use rand::distr::Open01;
let val: f32 = rand::rng().sample(Open01);
println!("f32 from (0, 1): {}", val);
```

# Bernoulli in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Bernoulli.html

`pub struct Bernoulli { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Bernoulli distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_distribution) `Bernoulli(p)`.

This distribution describes a single boolean random variable, which is true
with probability `p` and false with probability `1 - p`.
It is a special case of the Binomial distribution with `n = 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the Bernoulli distribution with `p = 0.1`,
`p = 0.5`, and `p = 0.9`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::distr::{Bernoulli, Distribution};
let d = Bernoulli::new(0.3).unwrap();
let v = d.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Bernoulli distribution", v);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#precision)Precision

This `Bernoulli` distribution uses 64 bits from the RNG (a `u64`),
so only probabilities that are multiples of 2-64 can be
represented.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct a new `Bernoulli` with the given probability of success `p`.

[§](https://docs.rs#precision-1)Precision

For `p = 1.0`, the resulting distribution will always generate true.
For `p = 0.0`, the resulting distribution will always generate false.

This method is accurate for any input `p` in the range `[0, 1]` which is
a multiple of 2-64. (Note that not all multiples of
2-64 in `[0, 1]` can be represented as a `f64`.)

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/bernoulli.rs.html#128)#### pub fn [from_ratio](https://docs.rs#method.from_ratio)(
    numerator: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    denominator: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/struct.Bernoulli.html), [BernoulliError](https://docs.rs/enum.BernoulliError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/rand/distr/bernoulli.rs.html#128)

#### pub fn [from_ratio](https://docs.rs#method.from_ratio)(
    numerator: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    denominator: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/struct.Bernoulli.html), [BernoulliError](https://docs.rs/enum.BernoulliError.html)>

Construct a new `Bernoulli` with the probability of success of
`numerator`-in-`denominator`. I.e. `new_ratio(2, 3)` will return
a `Bernoulli` with a 2-in-3 chance, or about 67%, of returning `true`.

return `true`. If `numerator == 0` it will always return `false`.
For `numerator > denominator` and `denominator == 0`, this returns an
error. Otherwise, for `numerator == denominator`, samples are always
true; for `numerator == 0` samples are always false.

# rand_distr::weighted - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/weighted/index.html

## Expand description

Weighted (index) sampling

This module is a superset of [ rand::distr::weighted](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/weighted/index.html).

Multiple implementations of weighted index sampling are provided:

- `WeightedIndex`- `rand`- `O(log N)`sampling over- `N`weights. It also supports updating weights with- `O(N)`time.
- `WeightedAliasIndex`- `O(1)`sampling, but due to high construction time many samples are required to outperform- `WeightedIndex`
- `WeightedTreeIndex`- `O(log N)`sampling and update/insertion/removal of weights with- `O(log N)`time.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Weighted](https://docs.rs/struct.WeightedAliasIndex.html)- Alias - Index
- A distribution using weighted sampling to pick a discretely selected item.
- [Weighted](https://docs.rs/struct.WeightedIndex.html)- Index
- A distribution using weighted sampling of discrete items.
- [Weighted](https://docs.rs/struct.WeightedTreeIndex.html)- Tree - Index
- A distribution using weighted sampling to pick a discretely selected item.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Invalid weight errors

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Aliasable](https://docs.rs/trait.AliasableWeight.html)- Weight
- Weight bound for `WeightedAliasIndex`
- [Weight](https://docs.rs/trait.Weight.html)
- Bounds on a weight

# Normal in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Normal.html

`pub struct Normal<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) `N(μ, σ²)`.

The Normal distribution, also known as the Gaussian distribution or
bell curve, is a continuous probability distribution with mean
`μ` (`mu`) and standard deviation `σ` (`sigma`).
It is used to model continuous data that tend to cluster around a mean.
The Normal distribution is symmetric and characterized by its bell-shaped curve.

See [ StandardNormal](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardNormal.html) for an
optimised implementation for

`μ = 0` and `σ = 1`.[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x) = (1 / sqrt(2π σ²)) * exp(-((x - μ)² / (2σ²)))`

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following diagram shows the Normal distribution with various values of `μ`
and `σ`.
The blue curve is the [ StandardNormal](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardNormal.html) distribution,

`N(0, 1)`.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Normal, Distribution};
// mean 2, standard deviation 3
let normal = Normal::new(2.0, 3.0).unwrap();
let v = normal.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a N(2, 9) distribution", v)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

Implemented via the ZIGNOR variant 1 of the Ziggurat method.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct, from mean and standard deviation

Parameters:

- mean (`μ`, unrestricted)
- standard deviation (`σ`, must be finite)

Parameters:

- coefficient of variation (`cv = abs(σ / μ)`)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/normal.rs.html#224-226)#### pub fn [from_zscore](https://docs.rs#method.from_zscore)(&self, zscore: F) -> F

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/normal.rs.html#224-226)

#### pub fn [from_zscore](https://docs.rs#method.from_zscore)(&self, zscore: F) -> F

Sample from a z-score

This may be useful for generating correlated samples `x1` and `x2`
from two different distributions, as follows.

```
let mut rng = rand::rng();
let z = StandardNormal.sample(&mut rng);
let x1 = Normal::new(0.0, 1.0).unwrap().from_zscore(z);
let x2 = Normal::new(2.0, -3.0).unwrap().from_zscore(z);
```

`pub struct StandardNormal;`## Expand description

The standard Normal distribution `N(0, 1)`.

# SkewNormal in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.SkewNormal.html

`pub struct SkewNormal<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [skew normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew_normal_distribution) `SN(ξ, ω, α)`.

The skew normal distribution is a generalization of the
[ Normal](https://docs.rs/struct.Normal.html) distribution to allow for non-zero skewness.
It has location parameter

`ξ` (`xi`), scale parameter `ω` (`omega`),
and shape parameter `α` (`alpha`).The `ξ` and `ω` parameters correspond to the mean `μ` and standard
deviation `σ` of the normal distribution, respectively.
The `α` parameter controls the skewness.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

It has the density function, for `scale > 0`,
`f(x) = 2 / scale * phi((x - location) / scale) * Phi(alpha * (x - location) / scale)`
where `phi` and `Phi` are the density and distribution of a standard normal variable.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the skew normal distribution with `location = 0`, `scale = 1`
(corresponding to the [ standard normal distribution](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardNormal.html)), and
various values of

`shape`.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{SkewNormal, Distribution};
// location 2, scale 3, shape 1
let skew_normal = SkewNormal::new(2.0, 3.0, 1.0).unwrap();
let v = skew_normal.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a SN(2, 3, 1) distribution", v)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

We are using the algorithm from [A Method to Simulate the Skew Normal Distribution](https://dx.doi.org/10.4236/am.2014.513201).

# Cauchy in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Cauchy.html

`pub struct Cauchy<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Cauchy distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_distribution) `Cauchy(x₀, γ)`.

The Cauchy distribution is a continuous probability distribution with
parameters `x₀` (median) and `γ` (scale).
It describes the distribution of the ratio of two independent
normally distributed random variables with means `x₀` and scales `γ`.
In other words, if `X` and `Y` are independent normally distributed
random variables with means `x₀` and scales `γ`, respectively, then
`X / Y` is `Cauchy(x₀, γ)` distributed.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x) = 1 / (π * γ * (1 + ((x - x₀) / γ)²))`

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The plot illustrates the Cauchy distribution with various values of `x₀` and `γ`.
Note how the median parameter `x₀` shifts the distribution along the x-axis,
and how the scale `γ` changes the density around the median.

The standard Cauchy distribution is the special case with `x₀ = 0` and `γ = 1`,
which corresponds to the ratio of two [ StandardNormal](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardNormal.html) distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Cauchy, Distribution};
let cau = Cauchy::new(2.0, 5.0).unwrap();
let v = cau.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Cauchy(2, 5) distribution", v);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

Note that at least for `f32`, results are not fully portable due to minor
differences in the target system’s *tan* implementation, `tanf`.

# Binomial in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Binomial.html

`pub struct Binomial { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [binomial distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution) `Binomial(n, p)`.

The binomial distribution is a discrete probability distribution
which describes the probability of seeing `k` successes in `n`
independent trials, each of which has success probability `p`.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(k) = n!/(k! (n-k)!) p^k (1-p)^(n-k)` for `k >= 0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot of the binomial distribution illustrates the
probability of `k` successes out of `n = 10` trials with `p = 0.2`
and `p = 0.6` for `0 <= k <= n`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Binomial, Distribution};
let bin = Binomial::new(20, 0.3).unwrap();
let v = bin.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a binomial distribution", v);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#numerics)Numerics

The implementation uses `f64` internally, which leads to rounding errors for big numbers.
For very large samples (`> 2^53`) the least significant bits of the output will not be random.
This means that something like `bin.sample(&mut rand::rng()) % 4` will not follow the correct distribution.
The more significant bits should be correctly distributed.

# Geometric in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Geometric.html

`pub struct Geometric { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [geometric distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_distribution) `Geometric(p)`.

This is the probability distribution of the number of failures
(bounded to `[0, u64::MAX]`) before the first success in a
series of [ Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/struct.Bernoulli.html) trials, where the
probability of success on each trial is

`p`.This is the discrete analogue of the [exponential distribution](https://docs.rs/struct.Exp.html).

See [ StandardGeometric](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardGeometric.html) for an optimised
implementation for

`p = 0.5`.[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(k) = (1 - p)^k p` for `k >= 0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the geometric distribution for various
values of `p`. Note how higher `p` values shift the distribution to
the left, and the mean of the distribution is `1/p`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Geometric, Distribution};
let geo = Geometric::new(0.25).unwrap();
let v = geo.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Geometric(0.25) distribution", v);
```

# Hypergeometric in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Hypergeometric.html

`pub struct Hypergeometric { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [hypergeometric distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_distribution) `Hypergeometric(N, K, n)`.

This is the distribution of successes in samples of size `n` drawn without
replacement from a population of size `N` containing `K` success states.

See the [binomial distribution](https://docs.rs/struct.Binomial.html) for the analogous distribution
for sampling with replacement. It is a good approximation when the population
size is much larger than the sample size.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(k) = binomial(K, k) * binomial(N-K, n-k) / binomial(N, n)`,
where `binomial(a, b) = a! / (b! * (a - b)!)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot of the hypergeometric distribution illustrates the probability of drawing
`k` successes in `n = 10` draws from a population of `N = 50` items, of which either `K = 12`
or `K = 35` are successes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Distribution, Hypergeometric};
let hypergeo = Hypergeometric::new(60, 24, 7).unwrap();
let v = hypergeo.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a hypergeometric distribution", v);
```

# LogNormal in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.LogNormal.html

`pub struct LogNormal<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [log-normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution) `ln N(μ, σ²)`.

This is the distribution of the random variable `X = exp(Y)` where `Y` is
normally distributed with mean `μ` and variance `σ²`. In other words, if
`X` is log-normal distributed, then `ln(X)` is `N(μ, σ²)` distributed.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following diagram shows the log-normal distribution with various values
of `μ` and `σ`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{LogNormal, Distribution};
// mean 2, standard deviation 3
let log_normal = LogNormal::new(2.0, 3.0).unwrap();
let v = log_normal.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from an ln N(2, 9) distribution", v)
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct, from (log-space) mean and standard deviation

Parameters are the “standard” log-space measures (these are the mean and standard deviation of the logarithm of samples):

- `mu`(- `μ`, unrestricted) is the mean of the underlying distribution
- `sigma`(- `σ`, must be finite) is the standard deviation of the underlying Normal distribution

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/normal.rs.html#311-335)#### pub fn [from_mean_cv](https://docs.rs#method.from_mean_cv)(mean: F, cv: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[LogNormal](https://docs.rs/struct.LogNormal.html)<F>, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.NormalError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/normal.rs.html#311-335)

#### pub fn [from_mean_cv](https://docs.rs#method.from_mean_cv)(mean: F, cv: F) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[LogNormal](https://docs.rs/struct.LogNormal.html)<F>, [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.NormalError.html)>

Construct, from (linear-space) mean and coefficient of variation

Parameters are linear-space measures:

- mean (`μ > 0`) is the (real) mean of the distribution
- coefficient of variation (`cv = σ / μ`, requiring`cv ≥ 0`) is a standardized measure of dispersion

As a special exception, `μ = 0, cv = 0` is allowed (samples are `-inf`).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/normal.rs.html#350-352)#### pub fn [from_zscore](https://docs.rs#method.from_zscore)(&self, zscore: F) -> F

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/normal.rs.html#350-352)

#### pub fn [from_zscore](https://docs.rs#method.from_zscore)(&self, zscore: F) -> F

Sample from a z-score

This may be useful for generating correlated samples `x1` and `x2`
from two different distributions, as follows.

```
let mut rng = rand::rng();
let z = StandardNormal.sample(&mut rng);
let x1 = LogNormal::from_mean_cv(3.0, 1.0).unwrap().from_zscore(z);
let x2 = LogNormal::from_mean_cv(2.0, 4.0).unwrap().from_zscore(z);
```

# Pareto in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Pareto.html

`pub struct Pareto<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Pareto distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_distribution) `Pareto(xₘ, α)`.

The Pareto distribution is a continuous probability distribution with
scale parameter `xₘ` ( or `k`) and shape parameter `α`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the Pareto distribution with various values of
`xₘ` and `α`.
Note how the shape parameter `α` corresponds to the height of the jump
in density at `x = xₘ`, and to the rate of decay in the tail.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Pareto;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Pareto::new(1., 2.).unwrap());
println!("{}", val);
```

# Poisson in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Poisson.html

```
pub struct Poisson<F>(/* private fields */)
where
    F:
```
[Float](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/float/trait.Float.html) + [FloatConst](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/float/trait.FloatConst.html),
    [StandardUniform](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardUniform.html): [Distribution](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)<F>;## Expand description

The [Poisson distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution) `Poisson(λ)`.

The Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution with
rate parameter `λ` (`lambda`). It models the number of events occurring in a fixed
interval of time or space.

This distribution has density function:
`f(k) = λ^k * exp(-λ) / k!` for `k >= 0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the Poisson distribution with various values of `λ`.
Note how the expected number of events increases with `λ`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Poisson, Distribution};
let poi = Poisson::new(2.0).unwrap();
let v: f64 = poi.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Poisson(2) distribution", v);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#integer-vs-fp-return-type)Integer vs FP return type

This implementation uses floating-point (FP) logic internally.

Due to the parameter limit `λ < `, it
statistically impossible to sample a value larger [Self::MAX_LAMBDA](https://docs.rs/struct.Poisson.html#associatedconstant.MAX_LAMBDA)[ u64::MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html#associatedconstant.MAX). As such, it
is reasonable to cast generated samples to

`u64` using `as`:
`distr.sample(&mut rng) as u64` (and memory safe since Rust 1.45).
Similarly, when `λ < 4.2e9` it can be safely assumed that samples are less
than `u32::MAX`.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/poisson.rs.html#185)#### pub const [MAX_LAMBDA](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.MAX_LAMBDA): [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html) = 1.844e19

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/poisson.rs.html#185)

#### pub const [MAX_LAMBDA](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.MAX_LAMBDA): [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html) = 1.844e19

The maximum supported value of `lambda`

This value was selected such that
`MAX_LAMBDA + 1e6 * sqrt(MAX_LAMBDA) < 2^64 - 1`,
thus ensuring that the probability of sampling a value larger than
`u64::MAX` is less than 1e-1000.

Applying this limit also solves
[#1312](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/issues/1312).

# Exp in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Exp.html

`pub struct Exp<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [exponential distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_distribution) `Exp(λ)`.

The exponential distribution is a continuous probability distribution
with rate parameter `λ` (`lambda`). It describes the time between events
in a [ Poisson](https://docs.rs/struct.Poisson.html) process, i.e. a process in which
events occur continuously and independently at a constant average rate.

See [ Exp1](https://docs.rs/struct.Exp1.html) for an optimised implementation for

`λ = 1`.[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x) = λ * exp(-λ * x)` for `x > 0`, when `λ > 0`.

For `λ = 0`, all samples yield infinity (because a Poisson process
with rate 0 has no events).

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the exponential distribution with
various values of `λ`.
The `λ` parameter controls the rate of decay as `x` approaches infinity,
and the mean of the distribution is `1/λ`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Exp, Distribution};
let exp = Exp::new(2.0).unwrap();
let v = exp.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Exp(2) distribution", v);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct a new `Exp` with the given shape parameter
`lambda`.

[§](https://docs.rs#remarks)Remarks

For custom types `N` implementing the [ Float](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/float/trait.Float.html) trait,
the case

`lambda = 0` is handled as follows: each sample corresponds
to a sample from an `Exp1` multiplied by `1 / 0`. Primitive types
yield infinity, since `1 / 0 = infinity`.The case `lambda = N::neg_zero()` returns an error, because `-0.0` is typically
produced through underflow of computations with a negative ideal result, and
because `1 / -0.0 = -infinity`.

# Exp1 in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Exp1.html

`pub struct Exp1;`## Expand description

The standard exponential distribution `Exp(1)`.

This is equivalent to `Exp::new(1.0)` or sampling with
`-rng.gen::<f64>().ln()`, but faster.

See [ Exp](https://docs.rs/struct.Exp.html) for the general exponential distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the exponential distribution with `λ = 1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Exp1;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Exp1);
println!("{}", val);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

Implemented via the ZIGNOR variant 1 of the Ziggurat method. The exact
description in the paper was adjusted to use tables for the exponential
distribution rather than normal.

# Weibull in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Weibull.html

`pub struct Weibull<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Weibull distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution) `Weibull(λ, k)`.

This is a family of continuous probability distributions with
scale parameter `λ` (`lambda`) and shape parameter `k`. It is used
to model reliability data, life data, and accelerated life testing data.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x; λ, k) = (k / λ) * (x / λ)^(k - 1) * exp(-(x / λ)^k)` for `x >= 0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the Weibull distribution with various values of `λ` and `k`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Weibull;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Weibull::new(1., 10.).unwrap());
println!("{}", val);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#numerics)Numerics

For small `k` like `< 0.005`, even with `f64` a significant number of samples will be so small that they underflow to `0.0`
or so big they overflow to `inf`. This is a limitation of the floating point representation and not specific to this implementation.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Gumbel in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Gumbel.html

`pub struct Gumbel<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Gumbel distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gumbel_distribution) `Gumbel(μ, β)`.

The Gumbel distribution is a continuous probability distribution
with location parameter `μ` (`mu`) and scale parameter `β` (`beta`).
It is used to model the distribution of the maximum (or minimum)
of a number of samples of various distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x) = exp(-(z + exp(-z))) / β`, where `z = (x - μ) / β`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the Gumbel distribution with various values of `μ` and `β`.
Note how the location parameter `μ` shifts the distribution along the x-axis,
and the scale parameter `β` changes the density around `μ`.
Note also the asymptotic behavior of the distribution towards the right.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Gumbel;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Gumbel::new(0.0, 1.0).unwrap());
println!("{}", val);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/gumbel.rs.html#44)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/gumbel.rs.html#93-102)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Distribution%3CF%3E-for-Gumbel%3CF%3E)### impl<F> [Distribution](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)<F> for [Gumbel](https://docs.rs/struct.Gumbel.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/gumbel.rs.html#93-102)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Distribution%3CF%3E-for-Gumbel%3CF%3E)

### impl<F> [Distribution](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)<F> for [Gumbel](https://docs.rs/struct.Gumbel.html)<F>

# Frechet in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Frechet.html

`pub struct Frechet<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Fréchet distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_distribution) `Fréchet(α, μ, σ)`.

The Fréchet distribution is a continuous probability distribution
with location parameter `μ` (`mu`), scale parameter `σ` (`sigma`),
and shape parameter `α` (`alpha`). It describes the distribution
of the maximum (or minimum) of a number of random variables.
It is also known as the Type II extreme value distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x) = [(x - μ) / σ]^(-1 - α) exp[-(x - μ) / σ]^(-α) α / σ`

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The plot shows the Fréchet distribution with various values of `μ`, `σ`, and `α`.
Note how the location parameter `μ` shifts the distribution along the x-axis,
the scale parameter `σ` stretches or compresses the distribution along the x-axis,
and the shape parameter `α` changes the tail behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Frechet;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Frechet::new(0.0, 1.0, 1.0).unwrap());
println!("{}", val);
```

# Zeta in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Zeta.html

`pub struct Zeta<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Zeta distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_distribution) `Zeta(s)`.

The [Zeta distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeta_distribution)
is a discrete probability distribution with parameter `s`.
It is a special case of the [ Zipf](https://docs.rs/struct.Zipf.html) distribution with

`n = ∞`.
It is also known as the discrete Pareto, Riemann-Zeta, Zipf, or Zipf–Estoup distribution.[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(k) = k^(-s) / ζ(s)` for `k >= 1`, where `ζ` is the
[Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function).

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the zeta distribution for various values of `s`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Zeta;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Zeta::new(1.5).unwrap());
println!("{}", val);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#integer-vs-fp-return-type)Integer vs FP return type

This implementation uses floating-point (FP) logic internally, which can
potentially generate very large samples (exceeding e.g. `u64::MAX`).

It is *safe* to cast such results to an integer type using `as`
(e.g. `distr.sample(&mut rng) as u64`), since such casts are saturating
(e.g. `2f64.powi(64) as u64 == u64::MAX`). It is up to the user to
determine whether this potential loss of accuracy is acceptable
(this determination may depend on the distribution’s parameters).

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

The zeta distribution has no upper limit. Sampled values may be infinite. In particular, a value of infinity might be returned for the following reasons:

- it is the best representation in the type `F`of the actual sample.
- to prevent infinite loops for very small `s`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

We are using the algorithm from
[Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4613-8643-8),
Section 6.1, page 551.

# Zipf in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Zipf.html

`pub struct Zipf<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The Zipf (Zipfian) distribution `Zipf(n, s)`.

The samples follow [Zipf’s law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law):
The frequency of each sample from a finite set of size `n` is inversely
proportional to a power of its frequency rank (with exponent `s`).

For large `n`, this converges to the [ Zeta](https://docs.rs/struct.Zeta.html) distribution.

For `s = 0`, this becomes a [ uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the Zipf distribution for `n = 10` and
various values of `s`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::Zipf;
let val: f64 = rand::rng().sample(Zipf::new(10.0, 1.5).unwrap());
println!("{}", val);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#integer-vs-fp-return-type)Integer vs FP return type

This implementation uses floating-point (FP) logic internally. It may be
expected that the samples are no greater than `n`, thus it is reasonable to
cast generated samples to any integer type which can also represent `n`
(e.g. `distr.sample(&mut rng) as u64`).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation-details)Implementation details

Implemented via [rejection sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rejection_sampling),
due to Jason Crease[1](https://jasoncrease.medium.com/rejection-sampling-the-zipf-distribution-6b359792cffa).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct a new `Zipf` distribution for a set with `n` elements and a
frequency rank exponent `s`.

The parameter `n` is typically integral, however we use type

`F: [Float]`and since our implementation requires a floating-point type.

# Gamma in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Gamma.html

`pub struct Gamma<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Gamma distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_distribution) `Gamma(k, θ)`.

The Gamma distribution is a continuous probability distribution
with shape parameter `k > 0` (number of events) and
scale parameter `θ > 0` (mean waiting time between events).
It describes the time until `k` events occur in a Poisson
process with rate `1/θ`. It is the generalization of the
[ Exponential](https://docs.rs/struct.Exp.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#density-function)Density function

`f(x) =  x^(k - 1) * exp(-x / θ) / (Γ(k) * θ^k)` for `x > 0`,
where `Γ` is the [gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function).

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the Gamma distribution with
various values of `k` and `θ`.
Curves with `θ = 1` are more saturated, while corresponding
curves with `θ = 2` have a lighter color.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Distribution, Gamma};
let gamma = Gamma::new(2.0, 5.0).unwrap();
let v = gamma.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Gamma(2, 5) distribution", v);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

When the shape (`k`) or scale (`θ`) parameters are close to the upper limits
of the floating point type `F`, the implementation may overflow and produce
`inf`. On the other hand, when `k` is relatively close to zero (like 0.005)
and `θ` is huge (like 1e200), the implementation is likely be affected by
underflow and may fail to produce tiny floating point values (like 1e-200),
returning 0.0 for them instead. The exact thresholds for this to occur
depend on `F`.

The algorithm used is that described by Marsaglia & Tsang 2000 1,
falling back to directly sampling from an Exponential for

`shape == 1`, and using the boosting technique described in that paper for
`shape < 1`.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_distr/gamma.rs.html#249-263)

# ChiSquared in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.ChiSquared.html

`pub struct ChiSquared<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [chi-squared distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chi-squared_distribution) `χ²(k)`.

The chi-squared distribution is a continuous probability
distribution with parameter `k > 0` degrees of freedom.

For `k > 0` integral, this distribution is the sum of the squares
of `k` independent standard normal random variables. For other
`k`, this uses the equivalent characterisation
`χ²(k) = Gamma(k/2, 2)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The plot shows the chi-squared distribution with various degrees of freedom.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{ChiSquared, Distribution};
let chi = ChiSquared::new(11.0).unwrap();
let v = chi.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a χ²(11) distribution", v)
```

# StudentT in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.StudentT.html

`pub struct StudentT<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Student t-distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%27s_t-distribution) `t(ν)`.

The t-distribution is a continuous probability distribution
parameterized by degrees of freedom `ν` (`nu`), which
arises when estimating the mean of a normally-distributed
population in situations where the sample size is small and
the population’s standard deviation is unknown.
It is widely used in hypothesis testing.

For `ν = 1`, this is equivalent to the standard
[ Cauchy](https://docs.rs/struct.Cauchy.html) distribution,
and as

`ν` diverges to infinity, `t(ν)` converges to
[.](https://docs.rs/struct.StandardNormal.html)

`StandardNormal`[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The plot shows the t-distribution with various degrees of freedom.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{StudentT, Distribution};
let t = StudentT::new(11.0).unwrap();
let v = t.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a t(11) distribution", v)
```

# FisherF in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.FisherF.html

`pub struct FisherF<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Fisher F-distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-distribution) `F(m, n)`.

This distribution is equivalent to the ratio of two normalised
chi-squared distributions, that is, `F(m,n) = (χ²(m)/m) / (χ²(n)/n)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The plot shows the F-distribution with various values of `m` and `n`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{FisherF, Distribution};
let f = FisherF::new(2.0, 32.0).unwrap();
let v = f.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from an F(2, 32) distribution", v)
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Beta in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Beta.html

`pub struct Beta<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Beta distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution) `Beta(α, β)`.

The Beta distribution is a continuous probability distribution
defined on the interval `[0, 1]`. It is the conjugate prior for the
parameter `p` of the [ Binomial](https://docs.rs/struct.Binomial.html) distribution.

It has two shape parameters `α` (alpha) and `β` (beta) which control
the shape of the distribution. Both `a` and `β` must be greater than zero.
The distribution is symmetric when `α = β`.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The plot shows the Beta distribution with various combinations
of `α` and `β`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Distribution, Beta};
let beta = Beta::new(2.0, 5.0).unwrap();
let v = beta.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Beta(2, 5) distribution", v);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Triangular in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Triangular.html

`pub struct Triangular<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [triangular distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_distribution) `Triangular(min, max, mode)`.

A continuous probability distribution parameterised by a range, and a mode (most likely value) within that range.

The probability density function is triangular. For a similar distribution
with a smooth PDF, see the [ Pert](https://docs.rs/struct.Pert.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the triangular distribution with various values of
`min`, `max`, and `mode`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Triangular, Distribution};
let d = Triangular::new(0., 5., 2.5).unwrap();
let v = d.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a triangular distribution", v);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Dirichlet in rand_distr::multi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/multi/struct.Dirichlet.html

`pub struct Dirichlet<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [Dirichlet distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution) `Dirichlet(α₁, α₂, ..., αₖ)`.

The Dirichlet distribution is a family of continuous multivariate
probability distributions parameterized by a vector of positive
real numbers `α₁, α₂, ..., αₖ`, where `k` is the number of dimensions
of the distribution. The distribution is supported on the `k-1`-dimensional
simplex, which is the set of points `x = [x₁, x₂, ..., xₖ]` such that
`0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ 1` and `∑ xᵢ = 1`.
It is a multivariate generalization of the [ Beta](https://docs.rs/struct.Beta.html) distribution.
The distribution is symmetric when all

`αᵢ` are equal.[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the 2-dimensional simplices for various 3-dimensional Dirichlet distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::multi::Dirichlet;
use rand_distr::multi::MultiDistribution;
let dirichlet = Dirichlet::new(&[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]).unwrap();
let samples = dirichlet.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{:?} is from a Dirichlet(&[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) distribution", samples);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# UnitSphere in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.UnitSphere.html

`pub struct UnitSphere;`## Expand description

Samples uniformly from the surface of the unit sphere in three dimensions.

Implemented via a method by Marsaglia 1.

For a distribution that also samples from the interior of the sphere,
see [ UnitBall](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitBall.html).

For a similar distribution in two dimensions, see [ UnitCircle](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitCircle.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the unit sphere as a wireframe. The wireframe is meant to illustrate that this distribution samples from the surface of the sphere only, not from the interior.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{UnitSphere, Distribution};
let v: [f64; 3] = UnitSphere.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{:?} is from the unit sphere surface.", v)
```

# UnitDisc in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.UnitDisc.html

`pub struct UnitDisc;`## Expand description

Samples uniformly from the unit disc in two dimensions.

Implemented via rejection sampling.

For a distribution that samples only from the circumference of the unit disc,
see [ UnitCircle](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitCircle.html).

For a similar distribution in three dimensions, see [ UnitBall](https://docs.rs/struct.UnitBall.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the unit disc. This distribution samples individual points from the entire area of the disc.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{UnitDisc, Distribution};
let v: [f64; 2] = UnitDisc.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{:?} is from the unit Disc.", v)
```

# InverseGaussian in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.InverseGaussian.html

`pub struct InverseGaussian<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [inverse Gaussian distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_Gaussian_distribution) `IG(μ, λ)`.

This is a continuous probability distribution with mean parameter `μ` (`mu`)
and shape parameter `λ` (`lambda`), defined for `x > 0`.
It is also known as the Wald distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the inverse Gaussian distribution
with various values of `μ` and `λ`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{InverseGaussian, Distribution};
let inv_gauss = InverseGaussian::new(1.0, 2.0).unwrap();
let v = inv_gauss.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a inverse Gaussian(1, 2) distribution", v);
```

# NormalInverseGaussian in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.NormalInverseGaussian.html

`pub struct NormalInverseGaussian<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [normal-inverse Gaussian distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal-inverse_Gaussian_distribution) `NIG(α, β)`.

This is a continuous probability distribution with two parameters,
`α` (`alpha`) and `β` (`beta`), defined in `(-∞, ∞)`.
It is also known as the normal-Wald distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the normal-inverse Gaussian distribution with various values of `α` and `β`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{NormalInverseGaussian, Distribution};
let norm_inv_gauss = NormalInverseGaussian::new(2.0, 1.0).unwrap();
let v = norm_inv_gauss.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a normal-inverse Gaussian(2, 1) distribution", v);
```

# rand_distr::multi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/multi/index.html

## Expand description

Contains Multi-dimensional distributions.

The trait [ MultiDistribution](https://docs.rs/trait.MultiDistribution.html) supports multi-dimensional sampling without
allocating a

[for each sample.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`Vec`[is an extension for distributions with constant dimension.](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstMultiDistribution.html)

`ConstMultiDistribution`Multi-dimensional distributions implement `MultiDistribution<T>` and (where
the dimension is fixed) `ConstMultiDistribution<T>` for some scalar type
`T`. They may also implement `Distribution<Vec<T>>` and (where the
dimension, `N`, is fixed) `Distribution<[T; N]>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Dirichlet](https://docs.rs/struct.Dirichlet.html)
- The [Dirichlet distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution)`Dirichlet(α₁, α₂, ..., αₖ)`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Const](https://docs.rs/trait.ConstMultiDistribution.html)- Multi - Distribution
- An extension of `MultiDistribution`
- [Multi](https://docs.rs/trait.MultiDistribution.html)- Distribution
- A standard abstraction for distributions with multi-dimensional results

# rand_distr::uniform - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/uniform/index.html

## Expand description

A distribution uniformly sampling numbers within a given range.

[ Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html) is the standard distribution to sample uniformly from a range;
e.g.

`Uniform::new_inclusive(1, 6).unwrap()` can sample integers from 1 to 6, like a
standard die. [`RngExt::random_range`] is implemented over [.](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)

`Uniform`[§](https://docs.rs#example-usage)Example usage

```
use rand::RngExt;
use rand::distr::Uniform;
let mut rng = rand::rng();
let side = Uniform::new(-10.0, 10.0).unwrap();
// sample between 1 and 10 points
for _ in 0..rng.random_range(1..=10) {
    // sample a point from the square with sides -10 - 10 in two dimensions
    let (x, y) = (rng.sample(side), rng.sample(side));
    println!("Point: {}, {}", x, y);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#extending-uniform-to-support-a-custom-type)Extending `Uniform` to support a custom type

To extend [ Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html) to support your own types, write a back-end which
implements the

[trait, then implement the](https://docs.rs/trait.UniformSampler.html)

`UniformSampler`[helper trait to “register” your back-end. See the](https://docs.rs/trait.SampleUniform.html)

`SampleUniform``MyF32` example below.At a minimum, the back-end needs to store any parameters needed for sampling
(e.g. the target range) and implement `new`, `new_inclusive` and `sample`.
Those methods should include an assertion to check the range is valid (i.e.
`low < high`). The example below merely wraps another back-end.

The `new`, `new_inclusive`, `sample_single` and `sample_single_inclusive`
functions use arguments of
type `SampleBorrow<X>` to support passing in values by reference or
by value. In the implementation of these functions, you can choose to
simply use the reference returned by [ SampleBorrow::borrow](https://docs.rs/trait.SampleBorrow.html#tymethod.borrow), or you can choose
to copy or clone the value, whatever is appropriate for your type.

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand::distr::uniform::{Uniform, SampleUniform,
        UniformSampler, UniformFloat, SampleBorrow, Error};
struct MyF32(f32);
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
struct UniformMyF32(UniformFloat<f32>);
impl UniformSampler for UniformMyF32 {
    type X = MyF32;
    fn new<B1, B2>(low: B1, high: B2) -> Result<Self, Error>
        where B1: SampleBorrow<Self::X> + Sized,
              B2: SampleBorrow<Self::X> + Sized
    {
        UniformFloat::<f32>::new(low.borrow().0, high.borrow().0).map(UniformMyF32)
    }
    fn new_inclusive<B1, B2>(low: B1, high: B2) -> Result<Self, Error>
        where B1: SampleBorrow<Self::X> + Sized,
              B2: SampleBorrow<Self::X> + Sized
    {
        UniformFloat::<f32>::new_inclusive(low.borrow().0, high.borrow().0).map(UniformMyF32)
    }
    fn sample<R: Rng + ?Sized>(&self, rng: &mut R) -> Self::X {
        MyF32(self.0.sample(rng))
    }
}
impl SampleUniform for MyF32 {
    type Sampler = UniformMyF32;
}
let (low, high) = (MyF32(17.0f32), MyF32(22.0f32));
let uniform = Uniform::new(low, high).unwrap();
let x = uniform.sample(&mut rand::rng());
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.Uniform.html)
- Sample values uniformly between two bounds.
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformChar.html)- Char
- The back-end implementing `UniformSampler``char`.
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformDuration.html)- Duration
- The back-end implementing `UniformSampler``Duration`.
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformFloat.html)- Float
- The back-end implementing `UniformSampler`
- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformInt.html)- Int

- [Uniform](https://docs.rs/struct.UniformUsize.html)- Usize
- The back-end implementing `UniformSampler``usize`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- Error type returned from `Uniform::new``new_inclusive`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Sample](https://docs.rs/trait.SampleBorrow.html)- Borrow
- Helper trait similar to `Borrow``SampleUniform``SampleUniform`
- [Sample](https://docs.rs/trait.SampleRange.html)- Range
- Range that supports generating a single sample efficiently.

`UniformSampler`

- Helper trait handling actual uniform sampling.

# Pert in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.Pert.html

`pub struct Pert<F>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The [PERT distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PERT_distribution) `PERT(min, max, mode, shape)`.

Similar to the [ Triangular](https://docs.rs/struct.Triangular.html) distribution, the PERT distribution is
parameterised by a range and a mode within that range. Unlike the

[distribution, the probability density function of the PERT distribution is smooth, with a configurable weighting around the mode.](https://docs.rs/struct.Triangular.html)

`Triangular`[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot shows the PERT distribution with `min = -1`, `max = 1`,
and various values of `mode` and `shape`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand_distr::{Pert, Distribution};
let d = Pert::new(0., 5.).with_mode(2.5).unwrap();
let v = d.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a PERT distribution", v);
```

# StandardGeometric in rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/0.6.0/rand_distr/struct.StandardGeometric.html

`pub struct StandardGeometric;`## Expand description

The standard geometric distribution `Geometric(0.5)`.

This is equivalent to `Geometric::new(0.5)`, but faster.

See [ Geometric](https://docs.rs/struct.Geometric.html) for the general geometric distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#plot)Plot

The following plot illustrates the standard geometric distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::prelude::*;
use rand_distr::StandardGeometric;
let v = StandardGeometric.sample(&mut rand::rng());
println!("{} is from a Geometric(0.5) distribution", v);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

Implemented via iterated
[ Rng::gen::<u64>().leading_zeros()](Rng::gen::%3Cu64%3E().leading_zeros()).

# rand_distr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_distr/latest/rand_distr/

## Expand description

Generating random samples from probability distributions.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-exports)Re-exports

This crate is a super-set of the [ rand::distr](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html) module. See the

[module documentation for an overview of the core](https://docs.rs/rand/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand/distr/index.html)

`rand::distr`[trait and implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Distribution.html)

`Distribution`The following are re-exported:

- The `Distribution``Iter`
- The `StandardUniform``Alphanumeric``Uniform``OpenClosed01``Open01``Bernoulli`
- The `weighted`

[§](https://docs.rs#distributions)Distributions

This crate provides the following probability distributions:

- Related to real-valued quantities that grow linearly
(e.g. errors, offsets):
- `Normal`- `StandardNormal`
- `SkewNormal`
- `Cauchy`

- Related to Bernoulli trials (yes/no events, with a given probability):
- `Binomial`
- `Geometric`
- `Hypergeometric`

- Related to positive real-valued quantities that grow exponentially
(e.g. prices, incomes, populations):
- `LogNormal`

- Related to the occurrence of independent events at a given rate:
- Gamma and derived distributions:
- `Gamma`
- `ChiSquared`
- `StudentT`
- `FisherF`

- Triangular distribution:
- `Beta`
- `Triangular`

- Multivariate probability distributions
- `multi::Dirichlet`
- `UnitSphere`
- `UnitBall`
- `UnitCircle`
- `UnitDisc`

- Misc. distributions
- `InverseGaussian`
- `NormalInverseGaussian`

- `pub use`- [num_traits](https://docs.rs/num-traits/0.2.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/num_traits/index.html);

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |

# num-traits 0.2.19 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/^0.2.9

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# rand 0.10.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/^0.10.0

# Rand

Rand is a set of crates supporting (pseudo-)random generators:

- Built over a standard RNG trait: `rand_core::RngCore`
- With fast implementations of both [strong](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[small](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators:`rand::rngs``chacha20``rand_xoshiro``rand_pcg``rand_sfc``rand_seeder`[rngs repo](https://github.com/rust-random/rngs/)
- `rand::rng`- `std`targets
- Direct support for seeding generators from the [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate

With broad support for random value generation and random processes:

- `StandardUniform`- `Uniform`- [more](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/distr/index.html)
- Samplers for a large number of non-uniform random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- Random processes (mostly choose and shuffle) via `rand::seq`

All with:

- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations thanks to contributions from the wide user-base

Rand **is not**:

- Small (LoC). Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Primarily a cryptographic library. `rand`does provide some generators which aim to support unpredictable value generation under certain constraints; see[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/SECURITY.md)for details. Users are expected to determine for themselves whether`rand`'s functionality meets their own security requirements.

Documentation:

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. Current `MAJOR.MINOR` versions are:

- Version 0.10 was released in February 2026.

See the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md) or [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html) for more details.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator; a significant portion of sequence and distribution functionality requires this
- `sys_rng`enables- `rand::rngs::SysRng`(uses the- [getrandom](https://crates.io/crates/getrandom)crate)
- `std_rng`enables- `rand::rngs::StdRng`(uses the- [chacha20](https://crates.io/crates/chacha20)crate)
- `thread_rng`(implies- `std`,- `std_rng`,- `sys_rng`) enables- `rand::rngs::ThreadRng`and- `rand::rng()`

Optionally, the following dependencies can be enabled:

- `chacha`enables- `rand::rngs::{ChaCha8Rng, ChaCha12Rng, ChaCha20Rng}`(uses the- [chacha20](https://crates.io/crates/chacha20)crate)

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

-
`simd_support`(experimental) enables sampling of SIMD values (uniformly random SIMD integers and floats). Since`std::simd`is not yet stable this feature requires nightly Rust and may cause build failures.
-
`unbiased`use unbiased sampling for algorithms supporting this option: Uniform distribution.(By default, bias affecting no more than one in 2^48 samples is accepted.) Note: enabling this option is expected to affect reproducibility of results.

## Portability

### Reproducibility

Achieving reproducible results requires not only deterministic algorithms with fixed inputs but also a commitment to stability of algorithms and some platform-specific considerations. A subset of `rand` does aim to support reproducibility; read more about this in the book: [Portability](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html).

### WebAssembly support

The [WASI](https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI/tree/main) and Emscripten
targets are directly supported. The `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target is not
*automatically* supported. To enable support for this target, refer to the
[ getrandom documentation for WebAssembly](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).
Alternatively, the

`sys_rng` feature may be disabled.# License

Rand is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://github.com/rust-random/rand/blob/master/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# serde_with 3.21.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_with/^3

# Custom de/serialization functions for Rust's [serde](https://serde.rs)

This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde's  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with) and with the improved

[-annotation. Some common use cases are:](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/serde_as/index.html)

`serde_as`- De/Serializing a type using the `Display`and`FromStr`traits, e.g., for`u8`,`url::Url`, or`mime::Mime`. Check`DisplayFromStr`
- Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
With `serde_as`large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.`[bool; 64]`,`Option<[u8; M]>`, and`Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>`are all supported, as[this examples shows](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
- Skip serializing all empty `Option`types with`#[skip_serializing_none]`
- Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using `with_prefix!``with_suffix!`
- Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great`into a`Vec<String>`. Check the documentation for`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`

### Getting Help

**Check out the  user guide to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**

For further help using this crate, you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.

## Use `serde_with` in your Project

```
# Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
```
The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
Check the [feature flags](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/feature_flags/index.html) section for information about all available features.

## Examples

Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.

`DisplayFromStr`

```
// This will serialize
Foo
// into this JSON
```
### Large and const-generic arrays

serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.

On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.

```
// This allows us to serialize a struct like this
let arrays:  = Arrays ;
assert!;
```
`skip_serializing_none`

This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

```
// This will serialize
Foo
// into this JSON
```
### Advanced `serde_as` usage

This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde's  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with).
More details about

`serde_as` can be found in the [user guide](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/index.html).

```
use Duration;
// This will serialize
Durations
// into this JSON
// and serializes
Bytes
// into this JSON
```

# average 0.16.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/average/^0.16

# average

Calculate statistics of a sequence iteratively in a single pass, using
constant space and avoiding numerical problems. The calculations can be
easily parallelized by using `merge`.

This crate works without `std`.

## Implemented statistics

- Mean and its error.
- Variance, skewness, kurtosis.
- Arbitrary moments.
- Minimum and maximum.
- Quantile.
- Histogram.

## Crate features

The following features are available:

- `libm`enables- `Quantile`(using floating point functions provided by- `libm`). This is enabled by default. If the- `std`feature is also enabled,- `std`is preferred over- `libm`.
- `std`enables- `Quantile`(using floating point functions provided by- `std`).
- `serde`enables serialization, via Serde version 1.
- `rayon`enables support for- `rayon::iter::FromParallelIterator`.
- `nightly`enables the use of const generics for a histogram implementation without macros. Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and compiler versions will be compatible.

## Related Projects

- `quantiles`

---

# rand_pcg 0.10.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_pcg/^0.10.0

# rand_pcg

Implements a selection of PCG random number generators.

PCG is a family of simple fast space-efficient statistically good algorithms for random number generation. [Melissa O'Neill, Harvey Mudd College, 2014].

The PCG algorithms are not suitable for cryptographic uses, but perform well
in statistical tests, use little memory and are fairly fast.
See the [pcg-random website](http://www.pcg-random.org/).

This crate depends on [rand_core](https://crates.io/crates/rand_core) and is
part of the [Rand project](https://github.com/rust-random/rand).

Links:

## Crate Features

`rand_pcg` is `no_std` compatible by default.

The `serde` feature includes implementations of `Serialize` and `Deserialize`
for the included RNGs.

## License

`rand_pcg` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# rand_distr 0.6.0-rc.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/0.6.0-rc.0

# rand_distr

Implements a full suite of random number distribution sampling routines.

This crate is a superset of the [rand::distr](https://rust-random.github.io/rand/rand/distr/index.html) module, including support
for sampling from Beta, Binomial, Cauchy, ChiSquared, Dirichlet, Exponential,
FisherF, Gamma, Geometric, Hypergeometric, InverseGaussian, LogNormal, Normal,
Pareto, PERT, Poisson, StudentT, Triangular and Weibull distributions.  Sampling
from the unit ball, unit circle, unit disc and unit sphere surfaces is also
supported.

It is worth mentioning the [statrs](https://github.com/statrs-dev/statrs) crate which provides similar functionality
along with various support functions, including PDF and CDF computation. In
contrast, this `rand_distr` crate focuses on sampling from distributions.

## Portability and libm

The floating point functions from `num_traits` and `libm` are used to support
`no_std` environments and ensure reproducibility. If the floating point
functions from `std` are preferred, which may provide better accuracy and
performance but may produce different random values, the `std_math` feature
can be enabled. (Note that any other crate depending on `num-traits` with the
`std` feature (default-enabled) will have the same effect.)

## Crate features

- `std`(enabled by default):- `rand_distr`implements the- `Error`trait for its error types. Implies- `alloc`and- `rand/std`.
- `alloc`(enabled by default): required for some distributions when not using- `std`(in particular,- `Dirichlet`and- `WeightedAliasIndex`).
- `std_math`: see above on portability and libm
- `serde`: implement (de)seriaialization using- `serde`

## Links

## Old Issues and Pull Requests

- All closed Issues and merged Pull requests from before 5.February.2025 (version 0.5.0) can be found in the [rand](https://github.com/rust-random/rand)repository where this crate used to be.

## License

`rand_distr` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

---

# rand_distr 0.4.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/0.4.3

# rand_distr

Implements a full suite of random number distribution sampling routines.

This crate is a superset of the [rand::distributions](https://rust-random.github.io/rand/rand/distributions/index.html) module, including support
for sampling from Beta, Binomial, Cauchy, ChiSquared, Dirichlet, Exponential,
FisherF, Gamma, Geometric, Hypergeometric, InverseGaussian, LogNormal, Normal,
Pareto, PERT, Poisson, StudentT, Triangular and Weibull distributions.  Sampling
from the unit ball, unit circle, unit disc and unit sphere surfaces is also
supported.

It is worth mentioning the [statrs](https://github.com/boxtown/statrs) crate which provides similar functionality
along with various support functions, including PDF and CDF computation. In
contrast, this `rand_distr` crate focuses on sampling from distributions.

## Portability and libm

The floating point functions from `num_traits` and `libm` are used to support
`no_std` environments and ensure reproducibility. If the floating point
functions from `std` are preferred, which may provide better accuracy and
performance but may produce different random values, the `std_math` feature
can be enabled.

## Crate features

- `std`(enabled by default):- `rand_distr`implements the- `Error`trait for its error types. Implies- `alloc`and- `rand/std`.
- `alloc`(enabled by default): required for some distributions when not using- `std`(in particular,- `Dirichlet`and- `WeightedAliasIndex`).
- `std_math`: see above on portability and libm
- `serde1`: implement (de)seriaialization using- `serde`

## Links

## License

`rand_distr` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# rand_distr 0.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/0.4.1

# rand_distr

Implements a full suite of random number distribution sampling routines.

This crate is a superset of the [rand::distributions](https://rust-random.github.io/rand/rand/distributions/index.html) module, including support
for sampling from Beta, Binomial, Cauchy, ChiSquared, Dirichlet, Exponential,
FisherF, Gamma, Geometric, Hypergeometric, InverseGaussian, LogNormal, Normal,
Pareto, PERT, Poisson, StudentT, Triangular and Weibull distributions.  Sampling
from the unit ball, unit circle, unit disc and unit sphere surfaces is also
supported.

It is worth mentioning the [statrs](https://github.com/boxtown/statrs) crate which provides similar functionality
along with various support functions, including PDF and CDF computation. In
contrast, this `rand_distr` crate focuses on sampling from distributions.

If the `std` default feature is enabled, `rand_distr` implements the `Error`
trait for its error types.

The default `alloc` feature (which is implied by the `std` feature) is required
for some distributions (in particular, `Dirichlet` and `WeightedAliasIndex`).

The floating point functions from `num_traits` and `libm` are used to support
`no_std` environments and ensure reproducibility. If the floating point
functions from `std` are prefered, which may provide better accuracy and
performance but may produce different random values, the `std_math` feature
can be enabled.

# rand_distr 0.4.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_distr/0.4.0

# rand_distr

Implements a full suite of random number distributions sampling routines.

This crate is a super-set of the [rand::distributions](https://rust-random.github.io/rand/rand/distributions/index.html) module, including support
for sampling from Beta, Binomial, Cauchy, ChiSquared, Dirichlet, exponential,
Fisher F, Gamma, Log-normal, Normal, Pareto, Poisson, StudentT, Triangular and
Weibull distributions, as well as sampling points from the unit circle and unit
sphere surface.

It is worth mentioning the [statrs](https://github.com/boxtown/statrs) crate which provides similar functionality
along with various support functions, including PDF and CDF computation. In
contrast, this `rand_distr` crate focusses on sampling from distributions.

Unlike most Rand crates, `rand_distr` does not currently support `no_std`.
